examples.everyday: After the service, a friend told me that the church's evangelization effort in the neighborhood has been mostly about serving meals.
examples.professional: Our diocese wants to focus its evangelization budget on parish catechism classes and on reaching families who have stopped coming to Mass.
examples.analytical: Pope John Paul II's call for a new evangelization raises a theological question: should the church proclaim the gospel anew to those who once heard it, or to cultures that have never received it?

nuance.analogy: Evangelization is like planting seeds in a field: the work is to spread the good news widely, but the growth belongs to God.
nuance.etymology: From 'evangelize' (from Late Latin 'evangelizare', from Greek 'euangelizesthai', to bring good news) plus the suffix '-ation' in its American spelling '-ization'.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling '-isation' instead of the American '-ization'
Confusing 'evangelization' with 'proselytization', which has a more negative sense
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb 'euangelizō' (to bring good news) is the root of this word. In the RSV, Luke 4:18 presents Jesus saying that he has been sent to preach good news to the poor. Mark 1:14-15 describes Jesus proclaiming the good news of God, and Matthew 28:19-20 commissions the disciples to make disciples of all nations.

traditions.view: Evangelization is rooted in worship, the sacramental life of the church, and the faithful witness of Christians, often expressed through liturgy, Scripture translation, and missionary communities.

Evangelization is the essential mission of the church, including proclamation, catechesis, sacramental life, and the transformation of culture, and it was emphasized in the call for a new evangelization by Pope John Paul II.

Evangelization centers on proclaiming the gospel so that people come to personal faith in Christ, often with an emphasis on individual conversion and church planting, with differences among Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Baptist, and Pentecostal groups.

senses.definition: Flatness, smoothness; the quality of being flat or level.
The quality of being even (of numbers).

core.definition: The quality of being flat, smooth, or level, or of being equal in amount or balance.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on EE. The final syllables are reduced to 'uhn-uhs,' so the -ness is a soft 'nuhs' sound, not a full 'ness.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a physical or mathematical quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evenness for surfaces and numbers, such as the evenness of paint or the evenness of a sample. In everyday talk people more often say flat, smooth, or level. In statistics and data science, evenness can describe how equally values are distributed across groups.

distinctions.note: Smoothness refers to the absence of bumps, while evenness refers to consistency across a surface or distribution.
Equality is about equal status or treatment, while evenness is about a level or balanced quality.

examples.everyday: I like the evenness of this new paint, because it covers the wall without any streaks.
examples.professional: We measured the evenness of the sample distribution before running the regression.
examples.analytical: The evenness of the data suggests that the sampling method was not biased toward any group.

nuance.analogy: Like a freshly poured layer of concrete that settles flat, evenness describes a surface or distribution with no bumps.
nuance.etymology: From even plus the suffix -ness, forming a noun of quality.
common_mistakes: Confusing evenness with equality; evenness describes balance or level quality, not fair treatment of people.
Pronouncing the ending as a full 'ness' instead of a reduced 'nuhs.'

senses.definition: A programming construct that waits for and dispatches events or messages.

core.definition: A program mechanism that waits for events or messages and runs the matching handler code for each one.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on VENT, and loop rhymes with 'hoop.' Do not stress loop more strongly than event in this compound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a standard term in software development.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use event loop in programming, especially in JavaScript, Node.js, Python asyncio, and GUI frameworks. Developers say things like 'the event loop is blocked' when code runs too long. Outside software, the phrase is not used.

distinctions.note: A general loop repeats code until a condition is met, while an event loop repeatedly waits for and dispatches events.
A thread is a separate path of execution, while an event loop is a single mechanism that handles many events, often on one thread.

examples.everyday: Our coworker says the app freezes because the event loop is busy with one slow task.
examples.professional: We should move the heavy computation off the event loop so the server can keep responding to requests.
examples.analytical: The event loop model explains why a single long-running callback can delay every other task in the system.

nuance.analogy: Like a receptionist who answers each incoming call in turn and sends it to the right person, the event loop takes each event and dispatches it to the right handler.
common_mistakes: Stressing loop as strongly as event, which makes the compound sound unnatural.
Confusing an event loop with a simple for loop; an event loop waits for events rather than counting through a fixed range.

senses.definition: A software architectural pattern promoting the production, detection, consumption of, and reaction to events.

core.definition: A software design pattern in which components communicate by producing, detecting and reacting to events.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'AR' in 'architecture', with a secondary stress on 'event'. The 'driven' ending is an unstressed 'uhn', not 'dry-ven'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term in system design, with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'event-driven architecture' in cloud computing, microservices and data engineering, usually in design discussions or architecture reviews. It is a common phrase in job descriptions and technical blogs. In casual talk, it would only come up when someone is describing a technical project.

distinctions.note: Architecture is the system-level design of how many components interact, while programming is the coding style used inside a component.
Request-response means one component asks and another answers directly, while event-driven architecture lets producers and consumers act without knowing each other.

examples.everyday: My friend works on an event-driven architecture at a logistics company, so their apps react to shipment updates.
examples.professional: We are moving the order system to an event-driven architecture so inventory services can react to purchases without tight coupling.
examples.analytical: An event-driven architecture trades the simplicity of direct calls for loose coupling, but it makes the system harder to reason about and debug.

nuance.analogy: An event-driven architecture is like a city with a central bulletin board: people post news, and anyone interested reacts without the sender calling each one.
nuance.etymology: Compound of event, driven (from drive, Old English drifan) and architecture (from Greek architektōn, 'master builder').
common_mistakes: Stressing 'driven' as 'dry-ven', as if it rhymes with 'oven'; the ending is 'DRIV-uhn'.
Placing the main stress on 'vent' instead of on 'AR' in 'architecture'.

senses.definition: In an everlasting manner; without end; forever.
Perpetually; constantly.
senses.example: She loved her grandmother everlastingly, even after the family moved far away.

core.definition: Forever and without end; in a way that continues permanently or for an endless time.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on LAS in 'lasting,' with the 'er' in 'ever' reduced to a weak schwa plus r. Say 'ing-lee' with a light ending, not 'ing-lee' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Strongly positive or emotional, often used for devotion or dramatic effect; can sound overwrought in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'everlastingly' mostly in literature, poetry, sermons, and formal speeches. In everyday conversation they would more often say 'forever' or 'always.' A natural reply to a grand declaration of love is a warm, simple 'Me too.'

distinctions.note: 'Forever' is common in everyday American speech, while 'everlastingly' is literary and more ornate.
'Eternally' is more abstract and used in theology and philosophy, while 'everlastingly' sounds more poetic and emotional.

examples.everyday: My mom has been everlastingly patient with me, even when I've been impossible.
examples.professional: The founder remains everlastingly committed to the mission, even as the company has grown.
examples.analytical: The poet describes the beloved as everlastingly present, a claim that raises questions about time and memory.

nuance.analogy: Like a song that keeps playing in the room long after the music has stopped, the feeling seems to go on without end.
nuance.etymology: From 'everlasting,' formed from 'ever' and 'lasting,' with the adverb ending '-ly.'
common_mistakes: Using it in casual talk where 'forever' would sound more natural.
Confusing it with 'eternally,' which is more abstract and philosophical.

senses.definition: To cry out suddenly, from some strong emotion.
To say suddenly and with strong emotion.

core.definition: To cry out suddenly, or to say something loudly, because of a strong emotion such as surprise, joy, or fear.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -SKLAYM. The initial sound is a reduced 'ik,' and the -sk- cluster is pronounced cleanly without a vowel between s and k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a loud, emotional outburst, often one of surprise or joy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exclaim mostly in writing and storytelling: 'She exclaimed, "Look at that!"' In casual speech people more often say yell, shout, or say. A natural reply to an exclamation is to ask what happened or to say 'What? Tell me.'

distinctions.note: Shout describes a loud voice without necessarily showing emotion, while exclaim emphasizes a sudden, emotional outcry.
Say is neutral and general; exclaim adds strong feeling and loudness.

examples.everyday: When I opened the door, my roommate exclaimed, 'You finally fixed the sink!' and I could hear the relief in her voice.
examples.professional: During the review, the manager exclaimed that the new dashboard finally showed the right numbers.
examples.analytical: The narrator exclaims at the moment of revelation, and that outburst marks the turning point of the whole argument.

nuance.analogy: To exclaim is like a kettle whistling suddenly: the feeling builds up and then bursts out loud and fast.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exclamare, 'to cry out,' from ex- 'out' and clamare 'to shout.'
common_mistakes: Using exclaim for everyday talking; it sounds dramatic in casual speech.
Putting the exclamation in quotes without a comma: 'She exclaimed, "Look!"' is the standard form.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind exclaim in Luke is anaphōneō (ἀναφωνέω), 'to cry out loudly.' In Luke 1:42, Elizabeth cries out with a loud voice when Mary greets her, showing the joy of the Spirit at the meeting of the two mothers. In Mark 6:49, the disciples cry out in fear when they see Jesus walking on the sea, mistaking him for a ghost.

exclaim.etymology: From Middle French *exclamer*, from Latin *exclamo* (“call out”), from *ex-* + *clāmō* (“to call”).

senses.definition: Designed or fitted for execution, or carrying into effect.
senses.example: The committee drafted an executive plan with clear steps for carrying out the merger.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or having responsibility for the day-to-day running of an organization, business, country, etc.
senses.example: executive act

senses.definition: Exclusive.
senses.example: She works in an office with an executive bathroom.

senses.definition: A chief officer or administrator, especially one who can make significant decisions on their own authority.
senses.example: Our company hired a new chief executive who could approve major budgets without board approval.

senses.definition: The branch of government that is responsible for enforcing laws and judicial decisions, and for the day-to-day administration of the state.
senses.example: The executive branch issued new guidelines for federal agencies, bypassing a long congressional debate.

senses.definition: A committee that manages the day-to-day running of an organization. An executive committee.
senses.example: She was on the executive of the Union of Democratic Mineworkers.

senses.definition: A process that coordinates and governs the action of other processes or threads; supervisor.
senses.example: The operating system's executive thread schedules and coordinates every other process running on the machine.

core.definition: A senior manager in a company or organization who makes major decisions and directs its day-to-day operations.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on ZEK. The first syllable is a quick, reduced ig, and the -ecu- is pronounced yuh. Learners often stress the last syllable or pronounce it EX-ec-you-tive.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. The word suggests power, prestige and high pay. As an adjective it also describes premium items such as an executive suite or an executive car.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use executive for senior business leaders, often called the C-suite, and for the executive branch of government. As an adjective it describes top-level roles or documents, such as executive assistant or executive summary. Calling a middle manager an executive is inaccurate; use manager or director. In casual talk, exec is common shorthand.

distinctions.note: Manager is a broad term for anyone who supervises people, while executive is reserved for senior leaders with major decision-making authority.
Administrator suggests running routine operations, often in schools, hospitals or government; executive suggests authority to set strategy for an organization.

examples.everyday: My sister just got promoted, so she's now one of the executives at her company.
examples.professional: Please send the executive summary to the leadership team before Thursday's board meeting.
examples.analytical: The executive power granted to the presidency raises questions about how much authority a single office should hold.

nuance.analogy: An executive is like a ship's captain: the person who decides the course, while the crew carries it out.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin executivus, 'carrying out', from Latin exsequi, 'to carry out'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable as ig-zek-yoo-TIVE instead of ig-ZEK-yuh-tiv.
Using executive for any manager or office worker; in American business talk it means senior leadership.
Using the full word exec in formal writing; write executive in reports and emails.

executive.etymology: From Middle French *executif*, from Latin *executivus*, from Latin *exsequi*, from ex- ‘out’ + sequi ‘follow’.

senses.definition: The act or practice of exhorting.
senses.example: The pastor's exhortation of the congregation to volunteer at the shelter filled the room with energy.

senses.definition: Language intended to give advice or to urge or encourage.
senses.example: Her coach's halftime exhortation was short, loud, and exactly what the team needed.

core.definition: A strong, earnest speech or piece of writing that urges someone to do something, often of a moral or motivational kind.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -tay-, and the final -tion is pronounced 'shun'. Keep the 'or' vowel clear and do not reduce the r in 'exhort'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It implies sincere, serious encouragement, often with a moral or spiritual tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exhortation in sermons, speeches, commencement addresses and formal writing. In normal conversation people say 'a pep talk' or 'a call to action'. A casual 'pep talk' is far more common for sports or work motivation, and exhortation sounds more solemn.

distinctions.note: A pep talk is informal and short, typically before a game or task, while an exhortation is more serious and formal.
A sermon is a formal religious talk on a text, while an exhortation may be any earnest urging, religious or secular.

examples.everyday: After the game, my coach gave us a short exhortation to keep our heads up.
examples.professional: The vice president's closing exhortation asked every manager to own their metrics.
examples.analytical: Paul's exhortation in Romans 12 moves from doctrine to practice, linking belief with concrete Christian conduct.

nuance.analogy: An exhortation is a verbal push on the back: it aims to move you forward, not just to inform you.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exhortatio, from exhortari 'to urge strongly'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'exhortation to do' instead of 'exhortation to action' or 'an exhortation to do something'.
Pronouncing the middle as 'hor-TAY' with weak stress, which makes the word sound unclear.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek paraklēsis, from parakaleō, means 'calling alongside' and can mean exhortation, encouragement or comfort. Acts 2:40 records Peter exhorting the crowd, Hebrews 13:22 calls the letter a word of exhortation, and Romans 12:8 names exhortation as a gift. These texts present exhortation as earnest, pastoral speech aimed at building up the church.
patterns: [C, U] an exhortation to do sth

exhortation.etymology: From Middle English *exhortacioun*, from Old French *exhortacion*, from Latin *exhortātiōnem*, accusative singular of *exhortātiō* (“encouraging; exhortation”), from *exhortor* (“to encourage, exhort”), from *ex* (“out of, from”) + *hortor* (“encourage”).

senses.definition: Voluntary migration from one's native land to another.
senses.example: Her expatriation to Paris in 1925 gave her the freedom to write without constant interruptions.

senses.definition: Forced expulsion of from one's native land to another.
senses.example: The government's expatriation of dissidents during the 1970s was condemned by human rights groups worldwide.

core.definition: Leaving one's native country to live permanently elsewhere, or being forced to leave or banished from one's homeland.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on AY, the syllable before -shun, and the first syllable carries secondary stress. In American speech the -tree- sounds like 'tree' with a strong r, and the -shun ending is unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general use, but it can be heavy or painful when it refers to forced exile or to giving up citizenship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expatriation mostly in formal or legal contexts, such as renouncing US citizenship, which is called expatriation in official language. In everyday talk they say 'moving abroad' or 'living overseas.' The word can also describe forced banishment, which carries a much more serious and emotional tone.

distinctions.note: Emigration is leaving one's country, viewed from the country of origin, while expatriation focuses on the person leaving and their loss or change of nationality.
Exile usually means being forced out of one's country for political reasons, while expatriation can be either voluntary or forced.

examples.everyday: My friend moved to Canada for work and calls it a kind of expatriation, half joking.
examples.professional: The HR office handles the paperwork for expatriation when employees relocate overseas for several years.
examples.analytical: Joyce's expatriation was both a voluntary act and a deliberate rejection of the cultural life he had been raised in.

nuance.analogy: Expatriation is like transplanting a tree: the roots are pulled from familiar soil, and the tree must grow in a new place.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ex- 'out of' and patria 'fatherland', through the medieval Latin expatriare 'to leave one's country'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'expatriate', which is the person rather than the act.
Using it in casual speech where 'moving abroad' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Of a person: able to be extradited.
Of an action or an offense: for which one can be extradited.
senses.example: an extraditable offense

core.definition: Able to be legally sent by one country to another for trial or punishment, such as a person or a crime.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, EK, and the final -able is a reduced syllable ending in a syllabic l, so it sounds like -buhl. Avoid pronouncing the middle syllables as strong vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a legal term used in criminal law, government, and news reporting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extraditable mostly in legal, political, and news contexts, such as a country's treaty obligations or a case involving a suspect abroad. In casual speech people would say the person could be sent back or could be extradited. The word describes a crime or person eligible for extradition rather than the act itself.

distinctions.note: Deportable refers to removing a non-citizen from a country under immigration law, while extraditable refers to transfer to another country for prosecution under a treaty.
Deport is a verb about sending someone out of a country, whereas extraditable is an adjective describing whether a person or offense qualifies for extradition.

examples.everyday: My cousin says the man arrested in Mexico might be extraditable, but nobody knows yet.
examples.professional: Our compliance team confirmed that the fraud charge is extraditable under the treaty with the UK.
examples.analytical: The court had to decide whether the political character of the offense made the defendant non-extraditable.

nuance.analogy: An extraditable person is like a package whose shipping label is valid under a treaty between two countries.
nuance.etymology: From extradite, based on Latin ex- meaning out and traditio meaning handing over.
common_mistakes: Confusing extraditable with deportable, which concerns immigration rather than treaty-based transfer for prosecution.
Stressing the middle syllable, as in ek-struh-DYE-tuh-bul.

senses.definition: Unblemished (figuratively or literally); clean and pure; innocent.
senses.example: one's fair name

senses.definition: Light in color, pale, particularly with regard to skin tone but also referring to blond and red hair.
senses.example: She had fair hair and blue eyes.

senses.definition: Just.
senses.example: He must be given a fair trial.

senses.definition: Adequate, reasonable, or decent, but not excellent.
senses.example: Their performance has been only fair.

senses.definition: Favorable, pleasant.
senses.example: The weather was fair today.

senses.definition: Not overcast; cloudless; clear.
senses.example: a fair sky

senses.definition: Free from obstacles or hindrances; unobstructed; unencumbered; open; direct; said of a road, passage, etc.
senses.example: a fair mark; in fair sight; a fair view

senses.definition: Without sudden change of direction or curvature; smooth; flowing; said of the figure of a vessel, and of surfaces, water lines, and other lines.
senses.example: The yacht's hull has a fair curve that cuts through the water smoothly.

senses.definition: Taken direct from an opponent's foot, without the ball touching the ground or another player.
senses.example: The umpire awarded a free kick after the defender took a fair catch.

senses.definition: Of a coin or die, having equal chance of landing on any side, unbiased.
senses.example: A fair coin has a 50% chance of landing on heads.

senses.definition: Favorable to a ship's course.
senses.example: With the wind astern, the sailing crew hoped the breeze would stay fair all day.

senses.definition: Between the baselines.
senses.example: The ball landed fair along the first-base line, and the runner raced home.

senses.definition: Not a no ball.
senses.example: The bowler's delivery was fair, so the umpire did not call a no ball.

senses.definition: Something which is fair (in various senses of the adjective).
senses.example: When will we learn to distinguish between the fair and the foul?

senses.definition: A fair woman; a sweetheart.
senses.example: Good morrow, my fair, will you walk with me to the abbey?

senses.definition: A community gathering to celebrate and exhibit local achievements.
senses.example: The town's harvest fair showcased prize-winning vegetables and handmade quilts from local families.

senses.definition: An event for public entertainment and trade, a market.
senses.example: Every spring the old fair brings jugglers, food vendors, and traveling merchants to the village square.

senses.definition: An event for professionals in a trade to learn of new products and do business, a trade fair.
senses.example: Our software team is exhibiting new analytics tools at the trade fair in Las Vegas next month.

senses.definition: A traveling amusement park (called a funfair in British English and a (traveling) carnival in US English).
senses.example: The whole town was at the fair, young and old, rich and poor.

senses.definition: To smoothen or even a surface (especially a connection or junction on a surface).
senses.example: Before painting, the carpenter will fair the seams between the boards with filler and sandpaper.

senses.definition: To bring into perfect alignment (especially about rivet holes when connecting structural members).
senses.example: The riveters had to fair the holes so the steel beams would line up precisely.

senses.definition: To make an animation smooth, removing any jerkiness.
senses.example: She spent the afternoon fairing the character's motion curves to remove jerky movement.

senses.definition: To construct or design with the aim of producing a smooth outline or reducing air drag or water resistance.
senses.example: The engineers fair the car's body panels to reduce drag at highway speeds.

senses.definition: To become fair (favorable, not stormy).
senses.example: By noon the storm clouds had passed, and the afternoon began to fair.

senses.definition: Clearly, openly, frankly, civilly, honestly, favorably, auspiciously, agreeably.
senses.example: He told us fair and square what the repairs would cost.

core.definition: Treating people equally and according to the rules, without favoritism or bias; reasonable and just.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a rhotic r; the vowel glides into a schwa-r sound, so say FAIR, not 'fay-er' or 'fair-uh'. Keep the r clearly audible at the end.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Calling something 'fair' praises it as just, though 'That's not fair!' is a very common complaint in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fair' constantly in everyday life, from 'Is that fair?' in arguments to 'Fair enough' as a way of agreeing to a reasonable point. In sports and games, 'fair' also means following the rules. Be careful not to confuse it with 'fare' (ticket price) in spoken and written English.

distinctions.note: 'Just' stresses moral rightness or legal correctness, while 'fair' stresses equal treatment and reasonable balance between parties.
'Impartial' means taking no side at all, usually for a judge or referee, whereas 'fair' describes outcomes and treatment that a person would regard as reasonable.
'Equitable' is formal and suggests fairness that takes individual circumstances into account, such as in distributing resources.

examples.everyday: My brother got the bigger room, and that just isn't fair.
examples.professional: Let's make the scoring rules fair for both teams before we launch the pilot.
examples.analytical: Rawls argues that a just society is one whose basic institutions are arranged so that its benefits and burdens are distributed fairly among its citizens.

nuance.analogy: A fair referee is like a scale with no thumb on it: it may weigh heavily, but it weighs honestly.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fæger, meaning beautiful or pleasing; the sense of just developed later.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'fair' (just) with 'fare' (the price of a ride or ticket) in writing.
Using 'fair' to mean 'light-skinned' or 'beautiful' in casual speech, where it can sound dated or loaded.

fair.etymology: From Middle English *fayr*, *faire*, from Old English *fæġer* (“beautiful”), from **fagr*, from Proto-Germanic **fagraz* (“appropriate, fitting, nice, suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European **peh₂ḱ-* (“to attach, join; agreement, settlement”).

senses.definition: The doctrine that all events are subject to fate or inevitable necessity, or determined in advance in such a way that human beings cannot alter them.
senses.example: Her fatalism about the election made her see no point in volunteering for campaigns.

core.definition: The belief that events are predetermined and cannot be changed, so people should accept whatever happens.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAY, the first syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, so say the second as tuh and the final as um, not with full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Often negative, suggesting passivity or resignation; in philosophical contexts it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fatalism in discussions of philosophy, religion, politics, and psychology, and sometimes in everyday talk about pessimism. Saying someone has a 'fatalistic attitude' is a mild criticism that they give up too easily. In casual speech, people more often say 'it's just fate' or 'whatever will be will be.'

distinctions.note: Determinism is the broader philosophical view that all events have causes; fatalism adds that outcomes are inevitable regardless of action.
Pessimism is an expectation of bad outcomes; fatalism is the belief that outcomes cannot be changed by effort.

collocations: fatalism in the face of disease

examples.everyday: My uncle has a real fatalism about his health; he says if it's his time, it's his time.
examples.professional: Our team's fatalism about the legacy code made people stop proposing improvements altogether.
examples.analytical: Stoic fatalism and Calvinist predestination both raise the question of whether human choice has any real effect on outcomes.

nuance.analogy: Like a train whose tracks are already laid, so the passenger can watch the scenery but never choose the route.
nuance.etymology: From fatal (from Latin fatum, fate) plus -ism; the suffix denotes a doctrine or belief system.
common_mistakes: Confusing fatalism with fatalistic as the noun; fatalism is the belief, fatalistic is the adjective.
Mispronouncing the stress as fa-TAL-iz-um.

senses.definition: One who maintains that all things happen by inevitable necessity; a person who believes in fatalism.
senses.example: My grandmother was a fatalist who believed every storm and illness had been decided long ago.

core.definition: A person who believes that events are predetermined and that human choices cannot change what will happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAY. The middle syllable is a reduced uh sound, and the ending is a short -ist, not -eest.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. Calling someone a fatalist often suggests they give up too easily or refuse to act, though it can also describe a calm acceptance of what cannot be changed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fatalist in conversation, news, and philosophy, usually to describe someone who shrugs at problems with a phrase like 'It was going to happen anyway.' It is a noun for a person; the adjective is fatalistic. In casual speech, people more often say someone has a 'what will be, will be' attitude.

distinctions.note: A pessimist expects bad outcomes but may still believe that effort can change them; a fatalist believes outcomes are fixed no matter what anyone does.
A determinist holds that events follow from prior causes in a lawful way; a fatalist holds that outcomes are fixed regardless of what we do, even without any causal explanation.

collocations: a fatalist attitude toward the weather

examples.everyday: My brother is such a fatalist; he says if the flight is meant to leave, it will leave.
examples.professional: I am not a fatalist about the migration. If we test each stage, we can still fix the pipeline before launch.
examples.analytical: A fatalist who argues that every outcome is fixed must still explain why deliberation seems to matter to what actually happens.

nuance.analogy: A fatalist is a passenger who believes the route is already drawn and the driver has no say.
nuance.etymology: From fatal plus -ist; ultimately from Latin fatum, 'that which has been spoken', from fari, 'to speak'.
common_mistakes: Using fatalist as an adjective; say fatalistic, as in 'a fatalistic attitude'.
Writing 'I am fatalist' without an article; say 'I am a fatalist' or 'I am fatalistic'.

senses.definition: To pity; to show pity for.

core.definition: To feel pity or sadness because someone else is having a difficult or unfortunate experience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'sorry' on its first syllable, with the 'r' clearly pronounced. The 'for' reduces to 'fer', and the phrase links into 'feel-SAHR-ee-fer'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can express sincere pity, but it can sound condescending if you say it to someone who does not want pity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I feel sorry for him or I don't feel sorry for them when they are talking about someone's bad luck or own mistakes. Saying it to someone who is dealing with a hard situation can sound patronizing, so feel for is often kinder. A natural reply is Yeah, it's been rough, or No, it's fine.

distinctions.note: Feel sorry for can imply pity from a distance; feel for implies more shared emotional understanding.
Pity is a noun or verb with a more formal, emotional tone; feel sorry for is the everyday spoken version.

examples.everyday: I feel sorry for the guy who lost his keys in the parking lot, because it's raining.
examples.professional: I feel sorry for the contractors who had to redo the work, but the schedule slipped because of their error.
examples.analytical: Rousseau argues that we feel sorry for others out of pity, a natural feeling that arises from our capacity to imagine their suffering.

nuance.analogy: Feeling sorry for someone is like standing at the edge of a river and watching someone struggle: you feel for them but you are still on the bank.
nuance.etymology: Feel from Old English fēlan; sorry from Old English sārig (distressed, grieved).
common_mistakes: Using 'to' instead of 'for' after feel sorry: say 'feel sorry for him', not 'feel sorry to him'.
Saying 'feel sorry about him', which is not idiomatic; use 'for' with a person.

senses.definition: Wild; untamed.
senses.example: In this region, the wild boars can be dangerous, but (perhaps counterintuitively) the feral hogs can be even worse.

senses.definition: Of an animal, wild but descended from domestic or captive ancestors; thus, in the wild, although not necessarily of the wild type.
senses.example: In this region, the wild boars can be dangerous, but (perhaps counterintuitively) the feral hogs can be even worse.

senses.definition: Having the characteristics of an animal; animal-like.
Of a person, contemptible; unruly; misbehaved.
senses.example: Stop acting like a feral brat and apologize to your sister right now.

senses.definition: Behaving in an out-of-control way due to enthrallment with a certain thought, behavior, person, etc.
senses.example: Since the new game launched, he's been feral, sleeping three hours a night and ignoring everyone.

senses.definition: That is a feral character; zoomorphic.
senses.example: The novel's villain is a feral creature who stalks the moors on all fours.

senses.definition: Deadly, fatal.
senses.example: The feral fever swept through the valley, killing children within days of the first symptoms.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the dead, funereal.
senses.example: The church bells tolled in a feral rhythm as the procession wound slowly toward the graveyard.

senses.definition: A domesticated (non-human) animal that has returned to the wild; an animal, particularly a domesticated animal, living independently of humans.
senses.example: Animal control officers trapped several feral cats behind the old warehouse last week.

senses.definition: A furry character in art or literature which has the appearance of a regular animal (typically quadrupedal), that may or may not be able to communicate with humans or "anthros".
senses.example: The story is about a group of ferals which have to explore the ruins of society after the humans die out.

core.definition: Of an animal, wild after living with people, or having fallen back into a wild state, such as a feral cat.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the r is pronounced clearly, as in American English. Avoid turning the final syllable into 'ee-ul'; it ends with a soft, reduced schwa-l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests wildness, disorder or danger, and it is used for animals and sometimes for people behaving in a wild way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'feral' for cats, dogs, hogs and other animals that were once domestic and now live wild, especially in cities or on farms. Used about people, it is strong and can sound insulting or dramatic, as in 'feral teenagers.' In everyday talk you might hear 'feral cat colony' at a shelter or a neighbor's comment about strays.

distinctions.note: Wild is the general word for not tamed; feral specifically means an animal that was domestic and returned to the wild.
A stray is usually a domestic animal that is lost or homeless and may still depend on people, while a feral animal has no contact with humans.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor feeds the feral cats behind the garage every evening.
examples.professional: The county animal services office tracks feral cat populations to plan its spay and neuter program.
examples.analytical: The author describes the protagonist's feral behavior as a loss of the social restraints that once shaped him.

nuance.analogy: A feral animal is like a houseplant that escapes into the woods and grows wild again.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fera, 'wild beast'.
common_mistakes: Using 'feral' as a synonym for any wild animal, when it specifically refers to formerly domestic animals.
Pronouncing the word with two syllables, as in 'FEER-ul'.

senses.definition: A type of trailer hitch, which consists of a horseshoe-shaped plate on a multidirectional pivot, with a locking pin to couple with the kingpin of a truck trailer.
senses.example: The mechanic greased the fifth wheel before hitching the trailer to the truck bed.

senses.definition: In full, fifth-wheel trailer: a large caravan or travel trailer that is connected to a pickup truck for towing by a hitch similar to the one described in sense 1 located in the center of the truck's bed.
senses.example: We towed our fifth wheel across three states on our summer road trip.

senses.definition: Anything superfluous or unnecessary.
senses.example: I felt like a fifth wheel when both of them started giggling and making out during dinner.

senses.definition: An unwanted person accompanying two couples on a double date.
(historical) A horizontal wheel or segment of a wheel above the front axle and beneath the body of a carriage, forming an extended support to prevent it from overturning.
senses.example: The carriage lurched over the rut, and the fifth wheel kept it from tipping.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A person who is unnecessary or unwanted because they are an extra member of a group, such as a third person tagging along with a couple.

pronunciation.tip: Compound nouns put the main stress on the first word, so say FIFTH louder than wheel. Non-native speakers often add a vowel after the final th of fifth, so keep the cluster /fɪfθ/ tight and do not add a sound after it.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The phrase suggests someone feels unwanted or superfluous, so it is usually used about yourself with a little humor or self-pity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this about themselves when they feel out of place, for example joining two friends on a date or a couple on a road trip. It is casual and common in everyday speech. A natural reply is 'Oh, come on, you're not a fifth wheel, we want you here.' Do not use it to describe a real vehicle part in casual talk unless you mean the trailer hitch.

distinctions.note: Third wheel is more common in American dating talk and describes an extra person when two people are a couple. Fifth wheel is broader and suggests you are not needed anywhere in the group.
Odd one out is neutral and describes someone who is different from the rest. Fifth wheel adds the feeling of being unnecessary.
Spare tire is informal and can mean an extra person, but it is more often a joke about body fat. Fifth wheel is the normal idiom for social situations.

collocations: the fifth wheel on the trip
make someone feel like a fifth wheel

examples.everyday: I'd feel like a fifth wheel if I tagged along on your date night.
examples.professional: Since the design team had already agreed on the plan, I felt like a fifth wheel in that meeting.
examples.analytical: Without a clear role in the argument, the silent observer becomes a fifth wheel, present but adding nothing to the moral question.

nuance.analogy: Like a spare tire kept in the trunk that nobody needs until the day nobody does.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with third wheel in contexts where the group is not a couple
Pronouncing the final th of fifth as a separate syllable or dropping it to f

senses.definition: Obvious and offensive; blatant; scandalous.
senses.example: a flagrant, unforgivably outrageous disregard for human life

core.definition: Obvious and shocking, especially a wrong or violation done openly without any attempt to hide it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FLAY. The final syllable is a weak schwa, and the r should be clear, not dropped.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; it stresses that something bad is obvious and unashamed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flagrant' often in news, sports, and workplace talk, for example 'a flagrant foul' or 'a flagrant violation'. In casual speech people may say 'blatant' or 'totally obvious'. It is strong, so use it when you mean the wrongdoing is clearly unacceptable.

distinctions.note: 'Blatant' is common in everyday speech and stresses obviousness; 'flagrant' adds a stronger sense of outrageous offense.
'Obvious' is neutral and can be harmless; 'flagrant' always describes something bad.

examples.everyday: That driver cut right in front of us, which was a flagrant move.
examples.professional: The manager's flagrant disregard for the safety rules led to the audit.
examples.analytical: The author treats the regime's flagrant hypocrisy as the central evidence of its moral collapse.

nuance.analogy: A red flag waved in plain view, impossible to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From Latin flagrans, 'burning,' from flagrare, 'to burn.'
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it as 'fla-GRANT' with stress on the second syllable.
Using it for mild errors; it means serious and obvious, so it sounds too strong for small mistakes.

flagrant.etymology: From Middle French *flagrant*, from Latin *flagrantem*, present participle of *flagrare* (“blaze, burn”).

senses.definition: Subject to irregular changes in quantity or quality.
A fluctuation.
senses.example: Despite the daily fluctuating in gas prices, the family kept their budget steady.

core.definition: Going up and down or changing irregularly in amount, level or quality over time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FLUK.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes change without judging whether it is good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fluctuating constantly for prices, temperatures, weight, income, moods and energy levels. It is often used with between or around, as in prices fluctuating between forty and fifty dollars. If the direction of change is clear, Americans usually say rising or declining instead.

distinctions.note: Variable describes something that can be different in each case; fluctuating emphasizes changes over time.
Volatile describes sharp, fast and unpredictable change, often in markets; fluctuating is milder and more neutral.
Erratic has a negative tone and suggests unreliable, irregular behavior; fluctuating describes change without judging it.

examples.everyday: My energy levels have been fluctuating a lot this week, so I'm trying to rest more.
examples.professional: Since the sales numbers are fluctuating from week to week, let's use a three-month average in the forecast.
examples.analytical: Fluctuating interest rates shaped the central bank's short-term choices, but its long-run goal of inflation control stayed fixed.

nuance.analogy: Fluctuating prices are like the tide: they rise and fall, and you can plan around the pattern.
nuance.etymology: From the verb fluctuate, from Latin fluctuatus, past participle of fluctuare, to wave, from fluctus, wave.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable or saying flook-choo-ating with equal stress.
Writing fluctuate about fifty dollars; Americans say fluctuate around or fluctuate between.

senses.definition: The quality of being fluent.

core.definition: The quality of speaking or writing a language easily, correctly and smoothly, without long pauses or hesitation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FLOO. The middle syllable -ent is reduced to uhnt, and the -ness ending is a reduced nuhs sound with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes a valued language skill.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always say fluency for this idea, so use fluency in conversation and writing. Fluentness is rare and can sound like a learner's coinage. In speech, you might say She speaks English with fluency or She's a fluent speaker.

distinctions.note: Fluency is the standard American noun for this quality, while fluentness is rare and less natural.
Proficiency is a measure of overall skill, often tested formally; fluency focuses on smooth, easy production of the language.
Eloquence describes persuasive, graceful speech, often in formal settings; fluency is about ease and smoothness in ordinary communication.

examples.everyday: Your English has improved so much since last year; your fluency is impressive now.
examples.professional: The hiring manager asked about my fluency in technical English, since the team works with partners overseas.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether fluency in a second language reflects deep understanding or only well-practiced speech.

nuance.analogy: Fluentness is like a river running over smooth stones: the words move along without catching.
nuance.etymology: From fluent, from Latin fluens, flowing, plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using fluentness instead of the standard American word fluency.
Saying fluent English without in, as in fluent in English rather than fluent English is not standard American speech.

senses.definition: The characteristic or quality of being foggy.

core.definition: The state of being foggy: thick mist in the air, or a vague, unclear feeling in the mind after tiredness or illness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the y as a clear ee sound. The ending is a reduced -nuhs, and the stress does not move when you add -ness.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing mental confusion, neutral when describing weather.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use fogginess for brain fog after illness, poor sleep, or stress. It sounds natural in everyday talk and in health conversations. A common reply is 'Yeah, I've had some fogginess since the flu.'

distinctions.note: Fogginess is a vague, muddled feeling; confusion is not knowing what is happening or what something means.
Haze is a light, dusty or smoky veil in the air; fogginess can describe thicker mist or a muddled mind.

examples.everyday: I'm still dealing with some fogginess from the cold medicine.
examples.professional: Engineers blamed the fogginess in the camera feed on condensation on the lens.
examples.analytical: The author's fogginess about key terms makes the argument hard to evaluate.

nuance.analogy: Like looking through a bathroom mirror after a hot shower, fogginess blurs what should be clear.
nuance.etymology: From foggy plus -ness; fog has a Scandinavian origin of uncertain date.
common_mistakes: Confusing fogginess with fogey or fogy, which are unrelated words for an old-fashioned person.
Saying a fogginess instead of simply fogginess in most contexts.

senses.definition: A van (or wagon) that serves as a restaurant kitchen to sell hot food to customers.
senses.example: The food truck parked outside the library serves tacos to hungry students at lunchtime.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see food,‎ truck.
A food delivery truck.
senses.example: The food truck delivered our order of pizzas to the office within twenty minutes.

core.definition: A large vehicle with a built-in kitchen that sells prepared food to customers on the street or at events.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TRUCK, and the American r is clear and retroflex. The vowel in 'truck' is short and relaxed, not 'trook.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and casual, often associated with creative, affordable meals.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'food truck' for a mobile restaurant that parks at offices, festivals, and street corners. People often say 'There's a great food truck near the park on Thursdays.' The word 'truck' here means a large vehicle, not a pickup. Some cities call them 'street food' or 'mobile kitchens' in formal rules.

distinctions.note: A food cart is usually pushed or towed and smaller, while a food truck is a motorized vehicle with a full kitchen.
A restaurant has a fixed building, while a food truck moves between locations.

examples.everyday: Let's grab lunch from that food truck by the library; their tacos are amazing.
examples.professional: The company hired a food truck for the team offsite, so nobody had to leave the campus.
examples.analytical: The rise of food trucks shows how small-scale food businesses can use mobility to avoid high rent in dense cities.

nuance.analogy: Like a restaurant kitchen on wheels, a food truck brings the meal to where people already gather.
nuance.etymology: 'Food' from Old English 'foda'; 'truck' from Latin 'trochus' (wheel) through French 'troque'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'food car' instead of 'food truck' in American English.
Mispronouncing 'truck' with a long oo vowel.

conversation.text: There's a taco food truck parked outside our office every Tuesday.
Let's hit the food trucks at the festival for lunch.
My friend quit her job to open a food truck.

senses.definition: A natural source of water; a spring.
senses.example: Hikers rested beside a cold fountain high in the mountains, where clear water bubbled from rock.

senses.definition: An artificial, usually ornamental, water feature (usually in a garden or public place) consisting of one or more streams of water originating from a statue or other structure.
senses.example: His house is right beside that fountain on Street 15.

senses.definition: The structure from which an artificial fountain can issue.
senses.example: The city repaired the stone fountain in the plaza, which had been dry for two years.

senses.definition: A reservoir from which liquid can be drawn.
senses.example: The pen's fountain held enough ink for three weeks of daily notes.

senses.definition: A source or origin of a flow (e.g. of favors or knowledge).
senses.example: Her grandmother was the fountain of family stories, and everyone came to her for history.

senses.definition: A roundel barry wavy argent and azure.
senses.example: The family's coat of arms bore a fountain above a silver chevron on a blue field.

senses.definition: A juggling pattern typically done with an even number of props where each prop is caught by the same hand that throws it.
senses.example: In the juggling workshop, we practiced the fountain with four clubs before trying the cascade.

senses.definition: A soda fountain.
senses.example: After school we walked to the old drugstore and ordered milkshakes at the soda fountain.

senses.definition: A drink poured from a soda fountain, or the cup it is poured into.
senses.example: She ordered a cherry lime fountain and sat by the window with her homework.

senses.definition: A ground-based firework that projects sparks similar to a water fountain.
senses.example: The kids lit a fountain on the driveway and its sparks sprayed across the lawn.

senses.definition: Anything that resembles a fountain in operation.
senses.example: The broken water main sent a fountain of mud across the intersection.

senses.definition: To flow or gush as if from a fountain.
senses.example: Lava fountained from the volcano.

core.definition: A decorative structure in a garden or public place that shoots water into the air or a basin.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, FOWN. The final syllable is a reduced tun, with the t often flapped or softened to a light d between vowels in casual speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; fountains suggest beauty, refreshment, and public places.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fountain for ornamental water features in parks, malls, and plazas, and for drinking fountains, which are common in schools and public buildings. In restaurants, a soda fountain can refer to a drink dispenser. Biblically and poetically, fountain can mean a source of life or water.

distinctions.note: A spring is a natural source of water coming from the ground; a fountain is usually artificial or ornamental.
Water fountain in American English usually means a drinking fountain in a public building; fountain alone more often means an ornamental water feature.

examples.everyday: Let's meet by the fountain in the park after lunch.
examples.professional: The fountain in the lobby was shut off for maintenance, so we took the stairs.
examples.analytical: Scripture repeatedly pictures God as a fountain of life, the source from which all life flows.

nuance.analogy: Like a faucet that never runs out, bubbling up from its own source.
nuance.etymology: From Old French fontaine, from Latin fontana, from fons, 'spring'.
common_mistakes: Confusing fountain with the natural word spring
Saying water fountain for a park fountain (Americans usually mean a drinking fountain)
Stressing the second syllable
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, a fountain usually means a spring or source of water, and it is a central image for God as the source of life. The Hebrew word maqor means spring or source, and the Greek word pege means spring or fountain. Psalm 36:9 says that with God is the fountain of life. Jeremiah 2:13 calls God the fountain of living waters that the people forsook for broken cisterns. Revelation 21:6 speaks of giving water from the spring of the water of life.

fountain.etymology: From Middle English; from Old French *fontaine* (whence modern *fontaine*); from Late Latin *fontana*, from Latin *fontanus*, *fontaneus*, adjectives from *fons* (“source, spring”).

senses.definition: The loose collection of fictional works pertaining to a particular fictional universe, including literary, film, or television series from various sources, generally when all authorized by a copyright holder or similar authority.
senses.example: the Star Wars franchise

senses.definition: The collection of organizations in the history of a sports team; the tradition of a sports team as an entity, extending beyond the contemporary organization.
senses.example: The Whalers' home city of Hartford was one of many for the franchise.

senses.definition: A business operating under such authorization, a franchisee.
senses.example: Our neighbor runs a franchise of the coffee chain across the street.

senses.definition: The right to vote at a public election or referendum; see: suffrage.
senses.example: Many citizens fought hard for the franchise before women finally gained it nationwide.

senses.definition: A right or privilege officially granted to a person, a group of people, or a company by a government.
senses.example: The city council awarded the bus company a twenty-year franchise to operate downtown routes.

senses.definition: An acknowledgment of a corporation's existence and ownership.
senses.example: The state granted the railroad its corporate franchise in 1851.

senses.definition: The authorization granted by a company to sell or distribute its goods or services in a certain area.
senses.example: McDonald’s has exported its franchise.

senses.definition: A legal exemption from jurisdiction.
senses.example: The ambassador's diplomatic franchise shielded him from local prosecution.

senses.definition: The membership of a corporation or state; citizenship.
senses.example: Under the charter, the franchise of the corporation included all members of the guild.

senses.definition: The district or jurisdiction to which a particular privilege extends; the limits of an immunity; hence, an asylum or sanctuary.
senses.example: Fugitives fled across the river into the abbey's franchise, beyond the sheriff's reach.

senses.definition: The positive influence on the buying behavior of customers exerted by the reputation of a company or a brand.
senses.example: Strong brand franchise helps the company keep customers even when prices rise.

senses.definition: Exemption from constraint or oppression; freedom; liberty.
senses.example: Grandmother spoke of the franchise of the open prairie, where no one told her what to do.

senses.definition: To confer certain powers on; grant a franchise to; authorize.
senses.example: The state legislature franchised the new utility to supply electricity to the county.

senses.definition: To give to others the rights to sell or distribute (goods or services).
senses.example: The soda company franchises its bottling plants to local partners across the country.

senses.definition: (rare) To set free; invest with a franchise or privilege; enfranchise.
senses.example: The old king franchised the captive prisoners and sent them home to their villages.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A business licensed by a larger company to sell its products or services under the company's name, usually in a local outlet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FRAN-chise, and keep the ch sound soft. The final s is pronounced z, and learners often say fran-KHEEZ or fran-CHISE with the wrong stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a franchise is a normal, respectable way to run a small business, though a chain can feel impersonal to some customers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use franchise mostly for a local restaurant, gym, or store that belongs to a national brand, such as a McDonald's or a Planet Fitness. People say they are thinking of buying a franchise or that a store is a franchise, meaning the owner pays fees to use the brand. In sports and entertainment, the same word also means a team or a series of movies, which is a separate sense.

distinctions.note: A chain is a group of outlets under one name, which may be owned directly by the company; a franchise is a single outlet owned by a separate person under license.
A branch is run directly by the parent company, while a franchise is independently owned and operated under a franchise agreement.

examples.everyday: My cousin bought a Subway franchise near the highway, so she works like crazy but she is her own boss.
examples.professional: Our legal team reviewed the franchise agreement before we signed the lease for the new location.
examples.analytical: A franchise model distributes financial risk between the brand owner and the local operator, which is why the arrangement persists across industries.

nuance.analogy: A franchise is like renting a proven recipe along with the restaurant's name: you do the cooking and the business, but you follow the brand's rules.
nuance.etymology: From Old French franchise, meaning freedom or privilege, from franc, free.
common_mistakes: Saying fran-KHEEZ with stress on the second syllable.
Confusing franchise (the business) with franchisee (the person who owns it), as in saying I am a franchise when you mean you own one.

franchise.etymology: From Middle English *franchise*, *fraunchise*, from Old French *franchise* (“freedom”), a derivative of *franc* (“free”).

conversation.text: That franchise has like ten movies now.
The Star Wars franchise is huge.
He's the best player in franchise history.

senses.definition: Time when one is not working.
senses.example: I love to play football in my free time.

core.definition: Time when you are not working, studying or obligated to do anything, and can do what you want.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TIME, which uses the American diphthong ai, like tyme. Do not add an e sound, and keep the m at the end clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive; people value it, so asking about someone's free time is a friendly small-talk move.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use free time casually in conversation, such as 'What do you do in your free time?' It is very common in small talk, job interviews and getting to know someone. In formal writing people may say leisure time or off-duty time. A natural reply is 'Mostly hiking and reading.'

distinctions.note: Spare time is time left over after your obligations, while free time is more general and can mean any period when you are not working.
Leisure is more formal or academic and emphasizes relaxation or recreation, while free time is everyday and casual.

examples.everyday: What do you like to do in your free time? I'm trying to get into pottery.
examples.professional: We protect free time for our engineers on Fridays so they can focus on long-term projects without meetings.
examples.analytical: Marx's contrast between necessary labor and free time asks whether modern workers ever gain the freedom to flourish outside their jobs.

nuance.analogy: Free time is like an open afternoon on your calendar, unclaimed by anyone else.
nuance.etymology: Free comes from Old English frēo; time comes from Old English tīma.
common_mistakes: Saying a free time as if it were countable; free time is usually uncountable, so say some free time.
Using at my free time; the natural preposition is in my free time.

senses.definition: An interpretation of probability in terms of frequency, often specifically as the limit of the relative frequency of an event as the sample size approaches infinity.
senses.example: Her statistics professor argued that frequentism and Bayesian methods answer different questions entirely.

core.definition: The view that probability means the long-run relative frequency of an event over many repeated trials.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FREE-, and the final -ism is a reduced, unstressed 'iz-um.' Learners often stress the second syllable or pronounce the 'qu' as a separate 'k' and 'w' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in statistics and the philosophy of science, often used when comparing competing schools of thought.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frequentism mainly in statistics courses, research papers and debates about how to interpret data. It is often contrasted with Bayesianism. In casual talk, people say 'the frequentist approach' rather than frequentism, and the term is never used in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Frequentism treats probability as long-run frequency and treats parameters as fixed, while Bayesianism treats probability as degree of belief updated with evidence.
Frequentism is the philosophy or school of thought, while frequentist is the person or the adjective describing methods that follow it.

examples.professional: Before we rerun the A/B test, we should agree whether our team follows frequentism or a Bayesian approach.
examples.analytical: Frequentism grounds probability in hypothetical repetitions of an experiment, which makes single events difficult to assign probabilities to, a point the Bayesian critics press hard.

nuance.analogy: Frequentism is like judging a coin by flipping it a thousand times and counting heads, rather than guessing its fairness from one toss and a hunch.
nuance.etymology: From frequent, from Latin frequens, meaning often, combined with the suffix -ism meaning a doctrine or system of belief.
common_mistakes: Confusing frequentism with frequency; frequentism is a philosophy of probability, not just a count.
Using the term casually in everyday talk where 'the frequency of' or 'how often' would be clearer.

senses.definition: An advocate of frequentism.
Of or pertaining to frequentism.
senses.example: The frequentist approach defines a probability as the long-run relative frequency of an event.

core.definition: A statistician who defines probability as the long-run frequency of events in repeated trials.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FREE. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, and the t sound is clear before the final ist.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It names a school of thought without praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frequentist in academic statistics, data science, and research methods. It is often contrasted with Bayesian in classes and papers. It is a precise term, so people use it when discussing methods, not in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: A Bayesian treats probability as a degree of belief updated with data, while a frequentist treats it as long-run frequency in repeated trials.
Frequentism is the philosophy or method itself, while frequentist names a person or describes something related to it.

examples.everyday: My roommate who studies math says she is a frequentist, so she does not like the way I talk about gut feelings.
examples.professional: Our analysis team uses a frequentist approach, so we report p-values and confidence intervals for each test.
examples.analytical: A frequentist interprets a confidence interval as a procedure that captures the true parameter in a stated proportion of repeated samples.

nuance.analogy: A frequentist is like a coin-flipper who trusts the long run: flip enough times and the proportion of heads settles where it should.
nuance.etymology: From frequent, from Latin frequens, crowded or repeated, plus the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Using frequentist as a general word for someone who is frequently present; it is a technical statistics term.
Confusing frequentist with frequency distribution, which is a table or graph.

senses.definition: A cover of minute ice crystals on objects that are exposed to the air. Frost is formed by the same process as dew, except that the temperature of the frosted object is below freezing.
senses.example: Frost covered the windshield overnight, so I scraped it before driving to work.

senses.definition: The cold weather that causes these ice crystals to form.
Coldness or insensibility; severity or rigidity of character.
senses.example: The frost in her voice made it clear she was not forgiving him.

senses.definition: A shade of white, like that of frost.
senses.example: frost:

senses.definition: A kind of light diffuser.
senses.example: The photographer placed a frost over the studio window to soften the harsh sunlight.

senses.definition: (dated) A disappointment; a cheat.
senses.example: Getting stuck with a broken blender after paying full price was a real frost.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To cover with frost.
senses.example: Last night's cold snap frosted the fields and left the pumpkins glittering white.

senses.definition: To become covered with frost.
senses.example: The grass frosts over every clear night once October arrives in the valley.

senses.definition: To coat (something, e.g. a cake) with icing to resemble frost.
senses.example: My daughter wants to frost the cupcakes with blue icing for her friend's party.

senses.definition: To anger or annoy.
senses.example: I think the boss's decision frosted him a bit.

senses.definition: To sharpen (the points of a horse's shoe) to prevent it from slipping on ice.
senses.example: The farrier will frost the horse's shoes before the icy trail ride this weekend.

senses.definition: To bleach individual strands of hair while leaving adjacent strands untouched.
senses.example: She asked the stylist to frost just the front strands for a subtle highlight.

core.definition: A thin layer of tiny ice crystals that forms on cold surfaces when the air temperature falls below freezing, or the cold weather that causes it.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the open 'aw' of cot-caught speakers in many areas, so say it like 'frawst'. Don't add an extra vowel before the st cluster. The r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in weather talk; can be poetic or suggest coldness and harshness in literature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frost for the white crystals on windows and grass on winter mornings, and they say 'frost warning' or 'hard frost' in weather reports. Gardeners watch the frost date closely. Figurative uses such as 'a frost in her manner' sound literary.

distinctions.note: Ice is solid water in general, while frost is a delicate layer of crystals formed from water vapor on cold surfaces.
Freeze means water turns solid at or below 32°F; frost is the crystal layer that can form without a full freeze.

examples.everyday: Scrape the frost off the windshield before you drive to work.
examples.professional: The farm sent an alert about a hard frost tonight, so the crew will cover the young plants.
examples.analytical: In the poem the frost is a symbol of a cold, unfeeling world that quietly covers everything.

nuance.analogy: Frost is like the thin white sugar dusting on a cold donut, forming gradually on a surface that is colder than the air around it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'forst', related to Old Norse 'frost' and German 'Frost', ultimately from a root meaning to freeze.
common_mistakes: Saying 'frost' with a long 'o', such as 'frohst', instead of the open 'aw' sound.
Confusing frost with 'snow', which is falling precipitation rather than a surface coating.
Using 'frost' as a verb for making ice, when the verb means to cover with frost or icing.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture frost is part of the cold of winter, often named alongside snow and ice as a sign of God's power over creation. The Hebrew word behind it is kerach (ice, frost), which the RSV renders in various ways in the poetry of creation and winter. Psalm 147:16 describes God spreading frost like ashes over the earth, a picture of his command over the seasons. Psalm 148:8 lists frost among the created things that praise the LORD, and Job 38:29 asks who gives birth to the frost of heaven, pointing to God's sovereignty over nature.

frost.etymology: From Middle English *frost*, from an unmetathesized variant of Old English *forst* (“frost”), from Proto-Germanic **frustaz* (“frost”), from Proto-Indo-European **prews-* (“to freeze; frost”).

senses.definition: Covered in frost; frosty.
senses.example: Eiswein is made from frosted grapes.

senses.definition: Translucent, appearing to be covered in frost.
senses.example: She installed frosted windows, since there was a clear view of her bathroom from her neighbor's bedroom.

senses.definition: Damaged by frost.
senses.example: Frosted fruit will be unsalable.

senses.definition: Extremely intoxicated.
senses.example: I was so frosted after drinking that 12-pack.

senses.definition: A kind of milkshake made with ice cream.
senses.example: At the diner, she ordered a strawberry frosted and sipped it through a straw.

core.definition: Covered with frost or a white, frost-like coating, such as frosted glass, or topped with frosting, such as frosted cookies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FROST. The -ed ending is a weak vowel, though in casual speech Americans often say it closer to 'FRAWST-id'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; frosted glass suggests privacy and frosted cookies suggest a treat.
nuance.usage_note: Very common in everyday talk about baked goods, windows and glass: 'frosted cupcakes', 'frosted windows'. In some regions, especially parts of the Midwest, 'frosted' is also a word for a thick milkshake made with ice cream.

distinctions.note: Frosty describes cold weather, a cold surface or a cold manner; frosted describes something that has been covered or treated with frost or frosting.
For cakes, Americans use frosted and iced in similar ways, but frosted is more common in home baking.

examples.everyday: She brought a box of frosted cookies to the potluck, and they disappeared in ten minutes.
examples.professional: The conference rooms have frosted glass panels, so people can't see into the offices but the space still feels open.
examples.analytical: The frosted panel diffuses the light, hiding fine detail while still letting the room feel bright and spacious.

nuance.analogy: Like a window breathed on in winter: you can see that light is there, but not the details.
nuance.etymology: From frost (Old English forst) plus the past participle ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Using frosted for cold weather; for that Americans say frosty.
Assuming frosted always means sweet; frosted glass is for privacy, not food.

senses.definition: In a fundamental or basic sense; reaching the very core of the matter.
senses.example: The two approaches differ fundamentally in how they treat missing data.

core.definition: At the most basic level; in a way that changes or affects the core nature of something.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on MEN, with light stress on fun. The -ally ending reduces to uh-lee, not a strong ALLY, so say the final syllables quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it signals a deep, important difference, so it carries weight. It is often used in arguments to mark a serious disagreement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fundamentally when they want to say something changes at the root, as in we fundamentally disagree or that changes things fundamentally. It is common in news, business and debate. In very casual speech, basically is the everyday word; fundamentally sounds deliberate and a bit serious, so save it for points you want to stress.

distinctions.note: Basically means in general or in simple terms and often works as a hedge; fundamentally means at the deepest level and stresses a real, core difference.
Essentially means in its nature or for the most part; fundamentally is stronger, suggesting the change touches the very root of something.
Radically means suddenly or extremely; fundamentally describes depth at the root, not necessarily speed or extremity.

examples.everyday: Honestly, a bike and a car are fundamentally different, so I'd never trade one for the other.
examples.professional: Our new pricing model fundamentally changes how we bill clients, so we need to brief sales before launch.
examples.analytical: Descartes's method fundamentally reshapes the question of knowledge by beginning with doubt rather than with trust in the senses.

nuance.analogy: Repainting a house changes its look, but fundamentally changing its frame changes what the house can hold up.
nuance.etymology: English adverb formed from fundamental (from Latin fundamentum, foundation) plus the suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Spelling it fundamentaly with one l; the -ally ending of adverbs from -al adjectives always has two l's.
Using fundamentally as a casual filler where basically sounds natural, which can make speech stiff.

senses.definition: A device to restrain speech, such as a rag in the mouth secured with tape or a rubber ball threaded onto a cord or strap.
senses.example: The police report described a rag gag found tied around the victim's mouth.

senses.definition: An order or rule forbidding discussion of a case or subject.
senses.example: The judge issued a gag order barring lawyers from discussing the case with reporters.

senses.definition: Any suppression of freedom of speech.
senses.example: Critics say the new law amounts to a gag on journalists and activists.

senses.definition: A joke or mischievous prank.
senses.example: My brother always pulls a gag on me at breakfast, usually involving fake spiders.

senses.definition: A device or trick used to create a practical effect; a gimmick.
senses.example: The magician's gag made the coin appear inside the child's ear.

senses.definition: A shocking or surprising thing.
senses.example: Honestly, his new haircut is an absolute gag, you won't believe it.

senses.definition: A convulsion of the upper digestive tract, caused by the gag reflex.
senses.example: The dentist warned that the impression material might trigger a gag.

senses.definition: Any member of the species Mycteroperca microlepis of groupers.
senses.example: The charter captain pulled a gag grouper from the reef, measuring nearly three feet long.

senses.definition: To experience the vomiting reflex.
senses.example: He gagged when he saw the open wound.

senses.definition: To cause to heave with nausea.
senses.example: The smell of burnt rubber made me gag every time I walked past the garage.

senses.definition: To restrain someone's speech by blocking his or her mouth.
senses.example: The kidnappers tried to gag the security guard so he could not call for help.

senses.definition: To pry or hold open by means of a gag.
senses.example: The dental assistant had to gag the child's mouth open before the X-ray.

senses.definition: To restrain someone's speech without using physical means.
senses.example: When the financial irregularities were discovered, the CEO gagged everyone in the accounting department.

senses.definition: To choke; to retch.
To astonish (someone); to leave speechless.
senses.example: The sudden announcement gagged the whole audience, leaving everyone speechless.

core.definition: To feel like vomiting, or to choke or retch on something, often from a bad smell or taste.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'a' vowel as in 'cat' with a hard 'g' at both ends. Keep the sound short and clipped, and do not add an extra vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative and vivid. It describes disgust or nausea, though it can be used humorously.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say gag casually when something smells or tastes disgusting, as in 'That milk smells so bad I almost gagged.' In noun form, gag usually means a joke or a prank, as in 'the movie is full of silly gags.' It can also mean a legal order that restricts speech, which is a formal use in news and law.

distinctions.note: Retch is more clinical and describes the physical heaving motion; gag is more everyday and can describe the feeling or near-vomiting.
Choke means that something blocks your airway; gag means your body reacts with a reflex, often from disgust or from something in your throat.

examples.everyday: That fish smelled so strong at the restaurant that I almost gagged.
examples.professional: The court issued a gag order, so nobody on the project team can talk about the case publicly.
examples.analytical: A gag order restricts speech about a case, which raises questions about how public trust and the right to a fair trial are balanced.

nuance.analogy: Gag is like a sudden alarm in your throat that goes off before your brain has time to think.
