nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly imitative of choking sounds.
common_mistakes: Using gag to mean always joking; the joke sense is a noun, and the verb means feeling nausea.
Pronouncing the vowel as a long 'ay' as in 'gage.'

gag.etymology: The noun is from Early Modern English *gagge*; the verb is from Middle English *gaggen*.

senses.definition: A device in which small objects tumble through a set of pegs, coming to rest in a pattern that approximates a normal distribution.
senses.example: In the statistics lecture, the professor dropped steel balls through a Galton board to demonstrate the bell curve.

core.definition: A device with rows of pegs in which balls drop and bounce randomly, piling into bins in a bell-shaped pattern that illustrates the normal distribution.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BOARD, and Galton has only secondary stress, so say GAL-ton with a light second syllable rather than GAL-TON. The final t in Galton is a clear t, not a flap, and the r in board is strongly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a teaching and demonstration device with no evaluative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in statistics, data science and math classes, often when explaining the central limit theorem. You will hear it in lectures and science museums more than in everyday talk. Many people also call it a bean machine or quincunx, but Galton board is the standard modern name.

distinctions.note: The normal distribution is the mathematical pattern; the Galton board is a physical device that produces an approximation of it.
Quincunx is Galton's original name for the same device, now mostly historical; Galton board is the usual term today.

collocations: drop balls into a Galton board
bins at the bottom of a Galton board
central limit theorem on a Galton board

examples.everyday: My daughter loved the Galton board at the science museum, watching hundreds of balls pile up in the middle.
examples.professional: For the onboarding talk, I'll run a quick Galton board simulation to show new analysts why averages settle into a bell curve.
examples.analytical: The Galton board makes the central limit theorem visible: each peg deflects a ball left or right, so many small independent choices converge to a normal shape.

nuance.analogy: Like a crowd of random coin flips that, added together, always settles into the same bell-shaped mound.
nuance.etymology: Named after Sir Francis Galton, the English scientist who described the device in the late 1800s.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable of Galton instead of the first
Confusing a Galton board with a normal distribution, which is the mathematical pattern rather than the physical device

senses.definition: (of a message etc) difficult to understand because it has been distorted; scrambled.
senses.example: The voicemail was so garbled by static that I could not tell who had called.

core.definition: Distorted or mixed up so that a message, sound, or text is hard to understand.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -led is one quick syllable with no full vowel, so say it as GAR-buld, not gar-BULD or gar-bul-ED.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something that has become unclear through noise, error, or distortion, and it is often used about communication that failed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use garbled for bad phone connections, radio transmissions, voicemails, text messages, and secondhand news reports. You might say 'Your message came through garbled.' A natural reply is 'Sorry, can you repeat that? It was garbled.'

distinctions.note: Muffled describes a sound that is dull or hard to hear because something covers it; garbled means the content itself is distorted or scrambled.
Scrambled often suggests deliberate encoding or mixing up parts; garbled suggests accidental distortion that makes the meaning unclear.
Jumbled means items are out of order or piled together; garbled refers to information that has been corrupted so it cannot be understood.

examples.everyday: Your voicemail was so garbled that I couldn't tell if you were coming to dinner.
examples.professional: The API response came back garbled because the character encoding didn't match.
examples.analytical: Historians often work with accounts that were garbled in transmission, passed through so many retellings that their original details are lost.

nuance.analogy: A garbled message is like a photocopy of a photocopy: each copy loses a bit, until the picture is blurry.
nuance.etymology: Garble comes from Italian garbellare, to sift, from Arabic gharbala, to sift.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as a separate word, gar-BULD, instead of one short syllable.
Using garbled for something that is simply loud or noisy; it refers to distortion of meaning.

senses.definition: An outdoor area containing one or more types of plants, usually plants grown for food or ornamental purposes.
senses.example: flower garden; herb garden; rose garden; vegetable garden

senses.definition: Such an ornamental place to which the public have access.
senses.example: You can spend the afternoon walking around the town gardens.

senses.definition: Taking place in, or used in, such a garden.
senses.example: garden party; garden path; garden spade

senses.definition: An ornamental garden featuring plants and other features to attract, house, conserve, benefit and/or display certain animals.
senses.example: butterfly garden; wild bird garden

senses.definition: A road, street, or similar thoroughfare, which sometimes occupies a former garden.
senses.example: 32 Windsor Gardens.

senses.definition: The twentieth Lenormand card.
senses.example: The Garden card in her Lenormand spread promised social gatherings and public recognition.

senses.definition: A cluster; a bunch.
senses.example: A garden of ripe grapes hung heavy over the trellis by the back door.

senses.definition: Pubic hair or the genitalia it masks.
To grow plants in a garden; to create or maintain a garden.
senses.example: I love to garden—this year I'm going to plant some daffodils.

senses.definition: To smoke marijuana.
senses.example: Some of the guys would garden in the van before every shift.

senses.definition: Of a batsman, to inspect and tap the pitch lightly with the bat so as to smooth out small rough patches and irregularities.
senses.example: Before facing the first delivery, the batsman took a moment to garden the pitch.

senses.definition: Common, ordinary, domesticated.
senses.example: The problem is a garden variety bug that any developer could fix quickly.

core.definition: An outdoor area, often near a house, where people grow flowers, vegetables, or other plants.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is often just a syllabic n with no vowel before it, so say it as GAR-dn, not GAR-den with two full syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Gardens suggest growing, beauty, relaxation, and care, and the word is warm in most contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say garden for a plot where you grow plants, such as a vegetable garden or flower garden. The lawn around a house is usually called the yard, so 'I'm mowing the yard' is normal, but 'I'm mowing the garden' would sound odd. Garden also appears as a verb, to garden, which is very common in American hobby talk. In casual slang, garden can also mean smoking marijuana, but that is informal and not appropriate in most settings.

distinctions.note: Yard in American English usually means the open ground around a house, often lawn, while garden means an area deliberately planted with flowers or food.
Orchard is a planted area of fruit or nut trees; garden is a more general space for plants, flowers, or vegetables.
A park is a public area for recreation, often with trees and lawns, while a garden is usually tended for plants themselves.

examples.everyday: We planted tomatoes in the garden this weekend, so we'll have plenty by August.
examples.professional: The company's campus includes a rooftop garden that the facilities team maintains.
examples.analytical: The garden in the Genesis account is more than a place; it is a symbol of God's providence and human responsibility for creation.

nuance.analogy: A garden is like a notebook of living things: you choose what goes in, you tend it over time, and it shows your care.
nuance.etymology: From Old French jardin, from a Germanic root meaning enclosure.
common_mistakes: Calling the lawn around a house a garden; Americans usually say yard for lawn.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'den' with a clear vowel; it is usually a syllabic n.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word gan means an enclosed garden or park. In Genesis 2:8 the LORD God plants a garden in Eden, and in Genesis 2:15 he places the man there to till and keep it, which presents the garden as a place of human work and care. In John 18:1 the Gospel of John says Jesus entered a garden across the Kidron brook, the place of his arrest, where the Greek word kēpos is used for garden.

senses.definition: Something, especially a cord or wire, used for strangulation.
senses.example: The mob boss was known for having his enemies executed with a garrote of piano wire.

senses.definition: (historical) An iron collar formerly used in Spain to execute people by strangulation.
senses.example: The museum displays an iron garrote that was used in Spain for executions long ago.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To execute by strangulation, to kill using a garrote.
senses.example: The murderer was sentenced to be garroted in the town square before a crowd.

senses.definition: To suddenly render insensible by semi-strangulation, and then to rob.
senses.example: The thief garroted the drunk man in the alley, then emptied his pockets while he lay unconscious.

core.definition: A cord, wire or similar device twisted around a person's neck to strangle them, used as a weapon or method of execution.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable. The first syllable is a weak 'uh', and the rr is a single American r with no trill. The ending rhymes with 'hot' or 'rot'. Some speakers say /ɡəˈɹoʊt/, but /ɡəˈɹɑt/ is the common American form.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative and violent. It suggests a deliberate, methodical killing, often in crime reporting or history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter garrote mainly in news about crime, true crime stories, history and descriptions of Spanish executions. In everyday speech people more often say strangle or choke. The verb garrote also exists, meaning to kill someone by strangling with such a device, but it is also rare. Spelling garotte is a variant that appears in some older texts.
word_family: garroter (noun, a person who uses a garrote)

distinctions.note: Strangle is the general, everyday word for killing or choking someone by squeezing the throat; garrote specifically means strangling with a cord, wire or similar tool.
Choke can mean accidentally blocking the airway, such as with food, while garrote always implies a deliberate attack with a tool.

examples.everyday: That true crime podcast was about a killer who used a garrote made from piano wire.
examples.professional: The forensic report describes a thin ligature mark that is consistent with a garrote rather than a rope or belt.
examples.analytical: Early modern Spanish executions by garrote staged the state's power on the body, turning strangulation into a public spectacle.

nuance.analogy: A garrote works like a tourniquet turned into a weapon: the same tightening motion, used to kill rather than to stop bleeding.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish garrote, meaning a stick, cudgel or tightening cord; the ultimate origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in GAR-ote; the stress falls on the second syllable.
Confusing it with garrison, which has a different meaning and pronunciation.

related: garroter (noun, a person who uses a garrote)

senses.definition: A measure; a standard of measure; an instrument to determine dimensions, distance, or capacity; a standard.
senses.example: The machinist used a precise gauge as the standard for every bolt in the batch.

senses.definition: An act of measuring.
An estimate.
Any instrument for ascertaining or regulating the level, state, dimensions or forms of things.
senses.example: The mechanic attached a pressure gauge to check the tire's air level.

senses.definition: A thickness of sheet metal or wire designated by any of several numbering schemes, with lower numbers indicating larger size.
senses.example: Sheet metal for the car's roof comes in 18 gauge, which is fairly thick.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of track gauge.
Ellipsis of loading gauge.
A semi-norm; a function that assigns a non-negative size to all vectors in a vector space.
senses.example: The proof relies on the gauge of the convex set, which is nonnegative and positively homogeneous.

senses.definition: The number of stitches per inch, centimetre, or other unit of distance.
senses.example: She knitted the sweater on size 4 needles, matching the pattern's stitch gauge exactly.

senses.definition: The quantity of plaster of Paris used with common plaster to make it set more quickly.
senses.example: For a quicker set, the contractor added a little gauge to the plaster mix.

senses.definition: That part of a shingle, slate, or tile, which is exposed to the weather, when laid; also, one course of such shingles, slates, or tiles.
senses.example: Each cedar shingle has a seven-inch gauge, so the roof overlaps evenly.

senses.definition: A unit of measurement which describes how many spheres of bore diameter of a shotgun can be had from one pound of lead; 12 gauge is roughly equivalent to.75 caliber.
senses.example: Under the old system, a 20 gauge shotgun fires lighter shot than a 12 gauge.

senses.definition: A shotgun (synecdoche for 12 gauge shotgun, the most common chambering for combat and hunting shotguns).
senses.example: He took his 12 gauge out to the field before dawn for the duck hunt.

senses.definition: A tunnel-like ear piercing consisting of a hollow ring embedded in the lobe.
senses.example: She wore a half-inch gauge in her earlobe, which stretched the hole over years.

senses.definition: Cannabis.
senses.example: He pulled out a little gauge and asked if anyone wanted to smoke.

senses.definition: Relative positions of two or more vessels with reference to the wind.
senses.example: A vessel has the weather gauge of another when on the windward side of it, and the lee gauge when on the lee side of it.

senses.definition: The depth to which a vessel sinks in the water.
senses.example: Loaded with grain, the barge's gauge measured nearly nine feet below the waterline.

senses.definition: To measure or determine with a gauge; to measure the capacity of.
senses.example: Before the long trip, the mechanic gauged the tire pressure to be safe.

senses.definition: To estimate.
senses.example: Nobody could gauge how many fans would show up for the rainy opening game.

senses.definition: To appraise the character or ability of; to judge of.
senses.example: A good coach can gauge a player's character within a few minutes of practice.

senses.definition: To draw into equidistant gathers by running a thread through it.
senses.example: For the skirt's waistband, gauge the fabric by running a thread along the top edge.

senses.definition: To mix (a quantity of ordinary plaster) with a quantity of plaster of Paris.
To chip, hew or polish (stones, bricks, etc) to a standard size and/or shape.

core.definition: Noun: an instrument or scale for measuring something, such as the fuel gauge in a car. Verb: to measure something precisely, or to estimate how something is likely to turn out.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, and the u is silent, so it sounds like 'gage' or 'age' with a G. Do not say 'GOW-jay' or add a second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is objective when it names a measuring device, and it sounds slightly more thoughtful when used as a verb meaning to estimate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gauge' constantly for car dashboards, tire pressure, and tools, so 'fuel gauge' and 'pressure gauge' are everyday phrases. As a verb, 'hard to gauge' or 'gauge the mood' is common in meetings and conversation. Spelling it 'guage' is a frequent error.

distinctions.note: A measure is the amount or the act of measuring in general, while a gauge is usually an instrument or a standard tool for measuring a specific quantity.
To estimate is to make a rough guess, while to gauge implies a more careful judgment, often informed by evidence or an instrument.

examples.everyday: The fuel gauge says we've got a quarter tank, so we should stop soon.
examples.professional: Can you gauge how many people will show up to the demo so we can book the room?
examples.analytical: A poll is an imperfect gauge of public opinion, since it captures only the views of those who answer.

nuance.analogy: A gauge is like a thermometer for something you cannot see directly, such as the level of gas in a tank.
nuance.etymology: From Old French jauge, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'guage', which is a common misspelling.
Pronouncing it with a long u or as two syllables, such as 'GOW-jay'.

gauge.etymology: From Middle English *gauge*, *gaugen*, from Anglo-Norman, *gauger*, from *gauge* (“gauging rod”), from **galgō* (“measuring rod, pole”), from Proto-Germanic **galgô* (“pole, stake, cross”), from Proto-Indo-European **ǵʰalgʰ-*, **ǵʰalg-* (“perch, long switch”).

senses.definition: Someone who gawks; someone who stares stupidly.
senses.example: A gawker pressed against the window while paramedics loaded the injured man into the ambulance.

core.definition: A person who stares openly and curiously at something or someone, often in a rude way, such as at an accident or a celebrity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel is a short 'ah' as in 'cot', since most Americans merge cot and caught. The final -er is a reduced, r-colored 'ur' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly negative. It suggests rude staring rather than polite interest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gawker' casually about crowds at traffic accidents, fires, or celebrity sightings, often with a little disapproval. Drivers slowing down to look at a wreck are called 'rubberneckers', a near-synonym. Calling someone a gawker can sound rude, so use it with friends rather than strangers.

distinctions.note: An onlooker simply watches, which is neutral, while a gawker stares rudely or with excessive curiosity.
Rubbernecker is nearly the same, but it is especially used for drivers who slow down to look at accidents.

examples.everyday: Don't be a gawker, just let the paramedics get through.
examples.professional: Please keep the lobby clear so nobody becomes a gawker during the demo.
examples.analytical: The crowd becomes gawkers rather than witnesses, reducing the event to a spectacle.

nuance.analogy: A gawker is like a passenger who slows down to stare at a wreck on the highway.
nuance.etymology: From gawk (to stare) plus the suffix -er; the origin of gawk is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing gawker with gawky, which means awkward and ungainly.
Using it for a polite, neutral observer, when the word implies rude staring.

senses.definition: The state of being ghastly.
A ghastly thing.
senses.example: The ghastliness of the flooded basement haunted him long after the water was pumped out.

core.definition: The quality of being horrible, terrible or deeply unpleasant to see or experience, often in a shocking way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, GAST, and make the g hard. The -ly sound is weak, so say 'lih', and the final -ness ends in a soft uh sound, not a full s vowel.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes something shocking, grim or horrible.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'ghastliness' in casual talk. They more often say 'awful', 'gross' or 'horrible'. It appears in literature, criticism and careful descriptions of disturbing scenes or events.

distinctions.note: 'Horror' names a strong fear or disgust, while 'ghastliness' describes the quality that causes it.
'Grisliness' focuses on gruesome details, while 'ghastliness' covers any horrible or shocking quality.
'Hideousness' emphasizes extreme ugliness, while 'ghastliness' can also mean something frightening or morally horrifying.

examples.everyday: The ghastliness of that last scene in the movie kept me awake all night.
examples.professional: Users were horrified by the ghastliness of the error page that appeared during the outage.
examples.analytical: Milton's hell depends on the ghastliness of its landscapes rather than on any explicit description of pain.

nuance.analogy: It is like a stain that looks worse the longer you stare at it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gǣstlic, meaning ghostly or frightening, from gǣst (spirit or ghost). The sense of horror developed later.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'ghastlyness', which is incorrect.
Confusing 'ghastly' with 'ghostly', since the words are close in appearance but differ in meaning.

senses.definition: A member of the ancient tribe of Gideon.

core.definition: A member of Gideons International, the Christian group that places Bibles in hotel rooms; also a follower of the biblical judge Gideon.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a lighter stress on 'nite.' The middle syllables are quick and weak, so do not pronounce each syllable equally.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to a religious group or person and is not insulting, but it is specialized.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Gideonite' mainly for members of Gideons International, a Protestant volunteer group famous for placing Bibles in hotel rooms. The dictionary sense about an ancient tribe is misleading, since Gideon was a judge in Israel and his followers were not a separate tribe. Most Americans would say 'a Gideon' or 'a member of the Gideons.'

distinctions.note: 'Gideon' names the biblical judge or the Gideons organization, while 'Gideonite' refers to a member or follower.
A Gibeonite was a member of a people in Joshua 9 who made a treaty with Israel, a different group entirely.

examples.everyday: A friend of mine is a Gideonite, and he drives around to put Bibles in motels.
examples.professional: The local Gideon chapter asked for volunteers to stock Bibles in the new hotel on Main Street.
examples.analytical: The Gideonite tradition of distributing Scripture reflects a Protestant emphasis on the Bible as a widely shared text.

nuance.analogy: A Gideonite is like a volunteer courier of the Scriptures, leaving the Bible on the nightstand for travelers.
nuance.etymology: From the name Gideon (Hebrew Gidh'on, possibly 'hewer' or 'one who cuts down') plus the suffix '-ite,' meaning a follower or member.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'Gideonite' with 'Gibeonite,' which refers to a different people in Joshua 9.
Assuming it refers to an ancient tribe; in modern American use it almost always means a member of Gideons International.
nuance.biblical_note: Gideon, in Hebrew Gidh'on, is a judge of Israel from the tribe of Manasseh whose story is told in Judges 6-8. Judges 6:11-12 describes an angel calling him a mighty man of valor while he hides from the Midianites. Judges 7:7 tells how God reduces his army to 300 men so that Israel cannot claim the victory for itself. Judges 6:36-40 recounts the sign of the fleece, in which God is asked to wet and dry the fleece as a test.

core.definition: A hilly region east of the Jordan River in the Bible, known for its good pastureland and for a healing balm.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GIL. The last two syllables are reduced to a light uh-d, so say GIL-ee-ud, not gil-EE-ahd.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In religious settings it carries a tone of comfort and healing because of the balm passage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet Gilead in Bible study, sermons, and the novel The Handmaid's Tale, where it is a fictional state. In church talk, people often say there is a balm in Gilead, a phrase from a famous spiritual that refers to healing and hope.

distinctions.note: Gilead the place is the Transjordan highland; Gilead in The Handmaid's Tale is a fictional state, not a real place.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study group is reading about Jacob and Laban, and everyone keeps mentioning Gilead.
examples.professional: In my seminar paper, I compare Gilead's role in Israel's tribal history with the settlement of Transjordan.
examples.analytical: Jeremiah's question about whether there is no balm in Gilead assumes the region's fame for healing, which makes his despair sharper.

nuance.analogy: Gilead works like a famous landmark in a story: its name carries meaning far beyond its map location.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew place name; the meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying gil-EE-ad
Confusing the Bible region with the fictional state in The Handmaid's Tale
nuance.biblical_note: Gilead is a mountainous region east of the Jordan, in the territory of tribes such as Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh. Genesis 31:47-48 links the name to Jacob and Laban's covenant heap. Jeremiah 8:22 refers to the balm of Gilead, a medicinal resin, to express the absence of healing for Judah. Judges 11:1 identifies Jephthah the Gileadite as a leader from this region.

senses.definition: A ruminant in the genus Giraffa of the African savannah with long legs, a highly elongated neck, yellow fur patterned with dark spots typically in the form of a network, and two or more horn-like projections called ossicones; the tallest living animal.
senses.example: At the zoo, the children gasped when the giraffe leaned down to eat leaves from the tree.

senses.definition: A giraffe unicycle.
senses.example: The street performer balanced on a giraffe unicycle, its tall wheel towering over the crowd.

senses.definition: A very tall individual.
A very tall woman.

core.definition: A very tall African animal with a long neck, long legs and a spotted coat, the tallest living land animal.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, RAF, with a short a as in cat. The first syllable is reduced to a light juh, not jee or jer, and the final f is clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it is often used warmly in talk about zoos, animals and children.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use giraffe in everyday talk about zoos, safaris, and kids' books. The plural is giraffes. The unicycle and laugh senses are slang or rare; do not use them outside of jokes or wordplay.

distinctions.note: The okapi is a shorter forest relative with striped legs, and it is less well known to most Americans.
Camelopard is an archaic name for the giraffe, so it sounds old-fashioned in modern speech.

examples.everyday: The kids were thrilled when the giraffe leaned down to eat leaves from the feeder.
examples.professional: Our conservation report used giraffe population trends to show the effects of habitat loss.
examples.analytical: The giraffe's long neck is often cited in evolutionary biology as an example of selection for feeding height, though the debate continues.

nuance.analogy: A giraffe's neck is like a telescope pointed toward the treetops.
nuance.etymology: From Arabic zarafa, passing through Italian giraffa and French girafe.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in JER-aff; the stress is on the second syllable.
Spelling it girafe, which is the French form, not the English spelling.

giraffe.etymology: From Middle French *giraffe*, from Italian *giraffa*, from Arabic *زُرَافَة*, from Classical Syriac *ܙܪܝܦܐ*, from *زُرْنَاپَا*.

senses.definition: That which girds, encircles, or encloses; a circumference.
senses.example: the girdle of the world

senses.definition: A belt or sash at the waist, often used to support stockings or hosiery.
senses.example: She fastened the silver girdle around her waist before walking onto the stage.

senses.definition: A garment used to hold the abdomen, hips, buttocks, and/or thighs in a particular shape.
senses.example: Her grandmother still wore a girdle under her dresses for every formal occasion.

senses.definition: The line of greatest circumference of a brilliant-cut diamond, at which it is grasped by the setting.
senses.example: The jeweler checked the girdle of the diamond for chips before setting the stone.

senses.definition: A thin bed or stratum of stone.
senses.example: Geologists found a thin girdle of limestone between two layers of shale.

senses.definition: The clitellum of an earthworm.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the worm's girdle appeared as a thick band near its head.

senses.definition: The removal or inversion of a ring of bark in order to kill or stunt a tree.
senses.example: The forester cut a girdle around the invasive maples to kill them slowly.

senses.definition: To gird, encircle, or constrain by such means.
senses.example: The wide leather belt girdled his waist as he climbed onto the tractor.

senses.definition: To kill or stunt a tree by removing or inverting a ring of bark.
senses.example: Beavers can girdle young aspens, leaving the trees to die over the next season.

core.definition: A tight, elastic undergarment that shapes and holds in the waist, hips and thighs.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GUR, with an r-colored vowel. The final -le is a syllabic l with a light uh, so say GUR-dl, not GUR-dull with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly dated; talking about girdles can feel personal or old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans now more often say shapewear, though girdle is still common in older speech and in stores' lingerie sections. The verb meaning to encircle is literary. The word can also be used in religious or literary contexts for a belt or sash at the waist.

distinctions.note: A corset is more rigid and structured and may extend up to the bust, while a girdle is more elastic and covers the hips and thighs.
Shapewear is the modern general term that includes girdles, bodysuits and other shaping garments.
A belt is worn outside clothing to hold up trousers or add style, while a girdle is an undergarment.

examples.everyday: My mom says she can't wear that tight dress without a girdle.
examples.professional: The department store's lingerie team restocked girdles and shapewear before the spring sale.
examples.analytical: Historians of fashion argue that the girdle shaped women's bodies toward narrow ideals, linking clothing to social expectations.

nuance.analogy: A girdle holds the body in place the way a snug rubber band holds a bundle of papers together.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gyrdel, from gyrdan, to gird.
common_mistakes: Using girdle for any kind of underwear; it means a specific shaping garment.
Using girdle for a pants belt; Americans say belt for that.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, the girdle is a belt or sash at the waist, and the RSV uses the word for both a practical and a symbolic item. The Hebrew word ezor and the Greek word zone both refer to a belt worn at the waist. Key passages: Matthew 3:4, where John the Baptist wears a leather belt around his waist; Isaiah 11:5, where righteousness and faithfulness are described as the belt around the coming ruler; and Ephesians 6:14, where truth is pictured as a belt that a believer fastens on as armor.

girdle.etymology: From Middle English *girdel*, *gerdel*, *gurdel*, from Old English *gyrdel*, from **gurdil*, from Proto-Germanic **gurdilaz* (“girdle, belt”), equivalent to *gird* + *le*.

senses.definition: Exuberantly or triumphantly joyful.
senses.example: The children were gleeful when the snow day announcement came over the radio.

core.definition: Showing open, delighted joy, often about something good or about someone else's trouble.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced 'fuhl', with the vowel almost silent. Do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive for pure delight, but negative when the joy is at someone's misfortune.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gleeful for children, kids on holidays, or people celebrating a win. When the joy is at someone else's expense, the word can sound mocking. It describes a person's expression or mood, so you can say 'a gleeful grin'.

distinctions.note: Happy is the general, neutral word for pleasure. Gleeful is stronger and more visible, with noisy or playful energy.
Elated is more formal and suggests high spirits after a success. Gleeful is livelier and often childlike.

examples.everyday: The kids were gleeful when they heard school was canceled because of the snow.
examples.professional: The sales team was gleeful after closing the biggest deal of the quarter.
examples.analytical: Her gleeful tone in the essay signals satire rather than sincere praise, which changes how the reader should judge the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a kid on the last day of school, running out the door with nothing to hold back the joy.
nuance.etymology: From glee (from Old English gleo, meaning entertainment or mirth) plus the suffix -ful.
common_mistakes: Using gleeful for quiet or calm happiness. The word implies open, energetic delight.
Mispronouncing it with a long 'a' in the second syllable. It is GLEE-fuhl.

senses.definition: To look at carefully; to scrutinize; to analyze.
senses.example: Please go over the reports to make sure we haven't missed anything.

senses.definition: (dated) To turn out successful; to be well-received.
senses.example: That song really went over with the audience.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see go,‎ over.
senses.example: I'm going over to my friend's house because I've already gone over my weekly quota.

senses.definition: To create a response or impression.
senses.example: Playing a radio in the office did not go over well with his coworkers.

senses.definition: To spray paint graffiti over someone else's graffiti.
senses.example: Someone went over our mural with gray paint overnight, erasing the whole thing.

senses.definition: To encompass or cover (a subject).
senses.example: In first period, we're going over the basics of cell biology.

senses.definition: To score a try.
senses.example: The winger went over in the corner to score the winning try.

senses.definition: To convert or switch sides.
senses.example: He went over to the finance department's side in this dispute.

senses.definition: (dated) To convert to Roman Catholicism.
senses.example: After years as a Methodist, Uncle Joe went over to Rome and never looked back.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To review or examine something carefully, especially to check it, explain it, or find mistakes.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable of over, OH, and the final -er is a reduced American r-colored vowel, so say OH-vur, not OH-ver. Linking the two words gives a smooth goh-OH-vur sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word for careful review, and it is positive when the goal is to catch errors or prepare.
nuance.usage_note: In American offices, 'go over' is a common way to ask for a review, as in 'Can we go over the budget before the call?' It is less formal than 'review' and 'examine', which suit written reports. It can also mean to be well-received, but in everyday talk the review sense is most useful. A natural reply is 'Sure, I'll send the file first.'

distinctions.note: Review is a more formal word for examining something in detail, often in writing or a formal process, while go over is more conversational.
Go through often means checking each item in a list or sequence, while go over focuses on understanding or reviewing the whole.

examples.everyday: Can we go over the directions one more time before we leave?
examples.professional: Let's go over the dashboard numbers in the meeting before we send them to finance.
examples.analytical: The argument must go over each premise carefully, since a single weak step undermines the whole conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like running your eyes slowly over a map before a trip, checking each route.
common_mistakes: Using 'go over' with 'to' as in 'go over to the report' when you mean review it; say 'go over the report'.
Confusing the review sense with the success sense ('the idea went over well' means it was well-received).

conversation.text: Let's go over the plan one more time before the meeting.
Can you go over my resume and give me some feedback?
How did your presentation go over with the client?
We went over our budget on the trip.
Let's go over the agenda before the client joins.
Can we go over the budget one more time?
Sorry, we're going to go over by a few minutes.

senses.definition: A position of balance between excess and deficiency.

core.definition: The ideal middle point between two extremes, avoiding both excess and deficiency, especially in ethics and moderation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of golden and the second word, MEEN, with a long e. Mean here is different from mean meaning unkind, even though they are pronounced the same.

nuance.connotation: Positive and formal, suggesting wisdom and balance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use golden mean mainly in philosophy, ethics, and education, following Aristotle's idea that virtue lies between extremes. In everyday talk people say happy medium or a good balance. In statistics, mean means average, so do not confuse the golden mean, which is a concept of balance, with an arithmetic average. A natural reply in a seminar is something like that's the golden mean, right.

distinctions.note: Golden ratio is a specific mathematical proportion of about 1.618, while golden mean is a philosophical or ethical idea of balance.
Happy medium is a casual phrase for a satisfactory compromise, while golden mean is formal and philosophical.

examples.everyday: I want to work hard without burning out, so I'm trying to find the golden mean.
examples.professional: Our team needs the golden mean: enough process to avoid errors, but not so much that delivery stalls.
examples.analytical: Aristotle defined virtue as the golden mean between excess and deficiency, so courage lies between cowardice and recklessness.

nuance.analogy: The golden mean is the balance point of a seesaw: lean too far either way and it tips, but in the middle it stays level.
nuance.etymology: A translation of Latin aurea mediocritas, Horace's phrase for a moderate, comfortable way of life.
common_mistakes: Confusing golden mean with a statistical mean or average.
Confusing golden mean with the golden ratio, which is a mathematical number.

senses.definition: US spelling of good humor.

core.definition: A cheerful, pleasant mood or temper, especially when you stay friendly despite difficulty or irritation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of 'humor.' The 'h' is often dropped in relaxed speech, sounding like 'YOO-mer,' and the final syllable is an American 'r'-colored 'er,' not 'or.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a friendly and patient temperament, and is often used to praise someone who handles stress well.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, the spelling is 'good humor,' without the 'u' used in British English. Americans also use 'in good humor' or 'with good humor' in writing, while speech more often uses 'in a good mood.' The phrase 'Good Humor' also names the ice cream truck brand familiar from American childhoods.

distinctions.note: Good mood is the everyday phrase; good humor is slightly more formal and suggests patience and friendliness.
Sense of humor is the ability to find things funny; good humor is a cheerful state of mind.
Good nature is a steady, kind temperament; good humor is a more temporary cheerful mood.

examples.everyday: She took the traffic delay with good humor and told jokes the whole way to the airport.
examples.professional: The team kept good humor through the long release night, which made the bug hunt much less miserable.
examples.analytical: Ancient ethics often treated good humor as a social virtue, a disposition that eases conflict and makes shared life possible.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm room, it makes everyone else more comfortable being near you.
nuance.etymology: 'Good' comes from Old English gōd; 'humor' comes through Old French from Latin umor, meaning moisture or fluid.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling 'humour' in American writing.
Using 'good humor' to mean a joke; in English it means a cheerful mood or temperament.

senses.definition: Something that is well worth the money paid for it.
senses.example: it's not cheap, it's good value

core.definition: Something that is well worth the money paid for it, offering quality, usefulness or benefits that exceed its price.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VAL, and the second syllable is a quick yoo sound, not a long oo. Keep good short and light.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals a smart purchase and practical good sense, though it does not imply the cheapest option.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say good value or worth the money, not value for money, which is mainly British. You might hear 'This is a good value' about a hotel, a product or a service. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I thought so too, it was worth it.'

distinctions.note: A bargain is something cheap or on sale, while good value refers to quality relative to price, even at a normal price.
Cheap means low price, often with low quality; good value means the quality justifies the price.
Worth is a more general idea of being deserving of effort or money; good value is a specific comparison of benefit and cost.

collocations: a good value for the price

examples.everyday: This hotel is a good value for the price, especially since breakfast is included.
examples.professional: The vendor's support tier looks like good value compared with building our own monitoring from scratch.
examples.analytical: A good value depends on comparing benefit with cost, not on the sticker price alone.

nuance.analogy: Good value is like a sturdy coat that lasts for years: the price was higher than the cheapest one, but it pays for itself in warmth.
nuance.etymology: Good comes from Old English gōd; value comes from Latin valere, to be strong or worth.
common_mistakes: Saying value for money, which sounds British; Americans say good value or worth the money.
Confusing good value with cheap; a good value can cost more if it delivers more.

senses.definition: Any of various grazing waterfowl of the family Anatidae, which have feathers and webbed feet and are capable of flying, swimming, and walking on land, and which are generally bigger than ducks.
senses.example: There is a flock of geese on the pond.

senses.definition: A female goose.
senses.example: The female goose guarded her nest at the edge of the pond all spring.

senses.definition: The flesh of the goose used as food.
senses.example: For Christmas dinner we roasted a goose with apples and fresh sage stuffing.

senses.definition: A silly person.
senses.example: Don't be such a goose; of course the bridge will hold your weight.

senses.definition: (historical) An old English board game in which players moved counters along a board, earning a double move when they reached the picture of a goose.
senses.example: Our grandmother taught us the old game of goose, where landing on the picture earned a double move.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To sharply poke or pinch the buttocks, or prod between the buttocks (of a person).
senses.example: My brother kept goosing me in the hallway until I finally shoved him back.

senses.definition: To stimulate; to spur.
senses.example: The new manager's bonus plan was meant to goose sales during the slow winter quarter.

senses.definition: To gently accelerate (a vehicle); to give repeated, small taps on the accelerator of (a vehicle); to feather the throttle of (a vehicle).
senses.example: She learned to goose the old pickup gently up the steep, icy hill.

senses.definition: To hiss (a performer) off the stage.
senses.example: Angry fans tried to goose the struggling singer off the stage after his terrible set.

core.definition: A large waterbird, bigger than a duck, with a long neck, webbed feet, and a loud honking call.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the long oo sound of food, and the word ends in a voiceless s like a hiss. The plural geese is pronounced /ɡis/, with a short vowel like the one in kiss.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the bird. In 'silly goose' the term is affectionate, and it can be a mild insult when used about a person who is foolish.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use goose for the bird in everyday talk, in parks, on farms, and in cooking, especially at holidays. The plural is geese, not gooses. As a person's nickname, silly goose is a gentle, teasing phrase that parents and friends often use. The verb meaning to poke someone's buttocks is informal and childish, and the verb meaning to tap a car's gas pedal lightly is common among drivers.

distinctions.note: Geese are generally larger, with longer necks and legs, while ducks are smaller and have shorter necks.
Swans are bigger and more graceful with much longer necks, while geese are sturdier and noisier.

examples.everyday: We're having roast goose for Christmas dinner if you can come over.
examples.professional: The wildlife biologist reported that the Canada goose population on the lake has doubled in five years.
examples.analytical: Geese migrate in V-shaped formations, which biologists often explain as an energy-saving aerodynamic strategy.

nuance.analogy: A goose is a sturdy, loud cousin of the duck.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gos, from a Proto-Germanic root shared with German Gans.
common_mistakes: Using the plural gooses instead of geese.
Pronouncing geese with the vowel of goose, instead of the short i sound of /ɡis/.

goose.etymology: From Middle English *goos*, *gos*, from Old English *gōs*, from **gans*, from Proto-Germanic **gans*, from Proto-Indo-European **ǵʰh₂éns*.

core.definition: An ancient region in northern Mesopotamia, along the Habor River, where the Assyrians settled captive Israelites.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable has a short a as in ran.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a historical and biblical place name.
nuance.usage_note: Gozan appears mainly in Bible study, ancient history, and archaeology. Americans usually mention the Assyrian context when they name it. It is rarely used in everyday conversation.

examples.everyday: We read about Gozan in 2 Kings, where the Assyrians sent captured Israelites to that region.
examples.professional: In the lecture, the archaeologist showed how Gozan connected to Assyrian trade and military routes.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the Israelites exiled to Gozan were eventually absorbed into surrounding peoples.

common_mistakes: Pronouncing it GO-zahn or GOZ-un; the stress belongs on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Gozan was a region in northern Mesopotamia on the Habor River, under Assyrian control. In 2 Kings 17:6 the king of Assyria settles captured Israelites in Halah and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes. 1 Chronicles 5:26 lists Gozan among the places to which the Reubenites, Gadites and half-tribe of Manasseh were carried into exile.

senses.definition: Drawn, pictorial.
senses.example: The design team has created a new graphic language for the promotional material of this campaign.

senses.definition: Explicit, vivid, descriptive, often in relation to depictions of sex or violence.
senses.example: We are not publishing these images because of the graphic nature of the content.

senses.definition: Relating to or reminiscent of graphic arts.
senses.example: The museum's graphic design exhibit showcased posters from the 1960s civil rights movement.

senses.definition: Having a texture that resembles writing, commonly created by exsolution, devitrification and immiscibility processes in igneous rocks.
senses.example: graphic granite

senses.definition: A drawing or picture.
senses.example: The textbook included a graphic showing how the heart's valves open and close.

senses.definition: A computer-generated image as viewed on a screen forming part of a game or a film etc.
senses.example: I've just played this new computer game: the graphics are amazing.

senses.definition: A moth of the subfamily Melipotini.
senses.example: The entomologist pinned the graphic moth beside a specimen from the Melipotini subfamily.

core.definition: Showing or describing something in clear, vivid detail, often shocking detail such as violence, injury or sex.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The last syllable is a short ik sound, not ike, and the middle vowel is quick and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Often negative, since graphic usually warns of disturbing detail. In design or art contexts it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use graphic constantly in content warnings and news, as in graphic violence or graphic images. At work it also means visual design, as in graphic designer or the graphics team. A graphic novel is a book with comic-style art, and the term is common in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Graphic describes vivid detail or pictorial design; graphical describes things related to graphs or visual computer displays, such as a graphical interface.
Explicit means stated fully and plainly; graphic adds sensory and often shocking detail.
Vivid is usually positive, describing bright imagery; graphic usually describes unpleasant detail.

examples.everyday: The movie has some graphic violence, so I wouldn't let the kids watch it.
examples.professional: Our graphic designer finished the banner, and the files are ready for the print vendor.
examples.analytical: Graphic depictions of suffering in war photography raise hard ethical questions about the viewer's consent.

nuance.analogy: Graphic is like a close-up camera lens: it shows every detail, including the ones you wish you had not seen.
nuance.etymology: From Latin graphicus, from Greek graphikos, of writing or drawing, from graphein, to write.
common_mistakes: Saying graphic card for the computer hardware; the standard term is graphics card.
Stressing the second syllable; it is GRA-fik.

graphic.etymology: From Latin *graphicus* (“belonging to painting or drawing”), from Ancient Greek *γραφικός* (“belonging to painting or drawing, picturesque, of or for writing; of style, lively”), from *γραφή* (“drawing, painting, writing, a writing, description, etc.”),…

senses.definition: A tract of land in which the dead are buried.
A final storage place for collections of things that are no longer useful or useable.
senses.example: After the merger, the old server racks became a graveyard for outdated software nobody wanted to delete.

senses.definition: The discard pile, in some trading card games.
senses.example: Before shuffling, I checked the graveyard to see which cards my opponent had discarded.

senses.definition: A period very early in the morning in which there is very little activity.
senses.example: graveyard shift, graveyard slot, graveyard watch

senses.definition: Synonym of suicide (“a beverage combining all available flavors at a soda fountain”).
senses.example: At the soda fountain, my nephew always orders a graveyard, mixing every flavor into one cup.

senses.definition: A team where players are sent when they are not useful, or a team where players become useless if sent there.
senses.example: Fans joked that the bench was the graveyard where the coach buried his worst players.

core.definition: An area of land where dead people are buried; a cemetery, especially a small or old one next to a church.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable, GRAYV, and the second syllable is a lighter yard with a clear r. Do not stress both parts equally or say GRAVE-yard with a weak second part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly somber. It can be used literally or metaphorically, which may sound dark or humorous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use graveyard for a small or older burial ground, especially near a church, while cemetery is the general and more formal word. The word is also used in phrases like graveyard shift, and in a metaphorical sense for a place where ideas or projects die.

distinctions.note: Cemetery is the general and formal term used in public records and most modern places. Graveyard is more informal and often suggests a smaller churchyard setting.
Churchyard specifically means the land around a church used for burials, while graveyard can refer to any burial ground.

examples.everyday: We walked through the old graveyard behind the church on Sunday afternoon.
examples.professional: The company's old software became a graveyard of unused features that nobody maintains.
examples.analytical: Ezekiel's vision of the valley of dry bones uses the image of graves and a graveyard to show God's power to restore life.

nuance.analogy: A graveyard for ideas is like a drawer where old sketches go to be forgotten.
nuance.etymology: From grave and yard, combining the Old English graef, a burial place, with the word for an enclosed area.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural in American speech.
Using graveyard for a cemetery in a formal or legal document, where cemetery is the usual word.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word qever means grave or tomb. Ezekiel 37:12-13 (RSV) describes God opening the graves of his people and bringing them up from them. Matthew 27:52-53 (RSV) reports that tombs were opened and holy people raised after Christ's death.

senses.definition: Animal fat in a melted or soft state.
Any oily or fatty matter.
senses.example: Wipe the grease off the stovetop before it hardens into a sticky film.

senses.definition: Shorn but not yet cleansed wool.
senses.example: The shearers delivered the grease wool to the mill before the spring rains began.

senses.definition: Inflammation of a horse's heels, also known as scratches or pastern dermatitis.
senses.example: The farrier treated the horse's grease in its heels with medicated ointment.

senses.definition: Money.
senses.example: Nobody in the band had enough grease to pay for the studio time.

senses.definition: Synonym of fat (“work containing much blank, profitable to the compositor”).
senses.example: The printers preferred the grease in the lengthy tables, since the blank space paid well.

senses.definition: To put grease or fat on something, especially in order to lubricate.
senses.example: Before the trip, I greased the squeaky hinges on the garden gate.

senses.definition: To bribe.
senses.example: The contractor greased the inspector with cash so the permit would clear quickly.

senses.definition: To cause to go easily; to facilitate.
senses.example: A friendly phone call greased the wheels and got the loan approved that week.

senses.definition: To perform a landing extraordinarily smoothly.
senses.example: To my amazement, I greased the landing despite the tricky crosswinds.

senses.definition: To kill.
senses.example: Don't let the mobster find out who greased his partner last night.

senses.definition: To have sexual intercourse with.
senses.example: The tabloid claimed the actor had greased the starlet during the film festival.

senses.definition: To affect (a horse) with grease, the disease.
senses.example: The vet said the mare had been greased, so we kept her out of the wet paddock.

senses.definition: To depart or slip away.
senses.example: When the meeting dragged on, Tom quietly greased out the back door.

core.definition: A thick, oily substance, such as melted animal fat from cooking or a lubricant used on machinery.

pronunciation.tip: The noun is pronounced with an s sound, /s/, at the end. The verb 'to grease' is pronounced with a z sound, /z/, so the two forms sound different.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for cooking and machinery; negative when it describes something greasy or slimy, such as a person who seems insincere.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use grease for cooking fat in a pan, for bacon grease, and for lubricant on car parts, as in 'grab some grease for the wheel bearings'. The verb 'grease' is used in phrases like 'grease the pan' or 'grease the wheels'. Calling someone 'greasy' is an informal insult for someone who seems slick or insincere.

distinctions.note: Oil is usually liquid at room temperature, while grease is thicker and semi-solid, which lets it stay in place on moving parts.
Fat is the solid or semi-solid substance in food or the body, while grease is usually melted fat or a lubricant.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the bacon grease out of the fridge? I want to fry the eggs in it.
examples.professional: Maintenance should grease the bearings every five hundred hours to avoid early failure.
examples.analytical: Engineers distinguish grease from oil because the thickener in grease keeps the lubricant in place under heavy load.

nuance.analogy: Like the smooth layer that keeps two moving gears from grinding against each other.
nuance.etymology: From Old French graisse, from Latin crassa, 'thick' or 'fat'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the verb 'grease' with an s sound, when it should be a z sound.
Calling someone 'a grease' as a personal insult, which is not natural; use 'greasy' as the adjective.

grease.etymology: From Middle English *grece*, from Anglo-Norman *craisse*, from Vulgar Latin **crassia*, noun derived from Latin *crassus* (“fat, thick”).

senses.definition: In a grievous manner, severely.

core.definition: In a way that causes great pain, harm or sorrow; severely, as in grievously injured or grievously wrong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, reduce the middle syllable, and end with a clear ly. Do not add extra syllables between the v and the s.

nuance.connotation: Negative and strong; it signals severe harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use grievously almost only in formal writing, news reports and legal contexts, as in grievously injured. In casual speech they say badly or seriously. It pairs with words like wounded, injured, mistaken or wronged.

distinctions.note: Badly is everyday and general, while grievously is formal and stresses severe harm or sorrow.
Seriously is common and neutral, while grievously is stronger and more dramatic.

examples.everyday: My cousin was grievously hurt in a fall, but she's home now.
examples.professional: The bug grievously affected our billing system, so we rolled back the release.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the nation was grievously wronged by its own leaders.

nuance.analogy: If bad is a bruise, grievously is a deep wound that takes a long time to heal.
nuance.etymology: From grievous plus -ly, from Old French grevos, from Latin gravis, heavy.
common_mistakes: Using grievously in casual speech, where badly or seriously sounds more natural.
Dropping the middle syllable, saying GREE-slee instead of GREE-vus-lee.

senses.definition: A cat, especially an elderly female.

core.definition: An old female cat; a cat, especially an elderly female, often used with affection or mock disdain.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MAL, and the final syllable is a reduced unstressed vowel, not a long "een." Many learners stress the first syllable instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly humorous; it can sound playful or slightly condescending toward an old woman, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in daily speech. You will meet it in older novels, poetry, or witty writing, where it is a colorful way to say "cat." Saying it about an actual pet in casual conversation would sound like a deliberate joke.

distinctions.note: "Cat" is the ordinary word; "grimalkin" is literary, old-fashioned and often playful.
A tabby is a cat with a striped or blotched coat, which describes appearance, while grimalkin describes an old female cat.

collocations: a grimalkin dozing by the fire

examples.professional: The marketing copy for the vintage pet food brand used the word grimalkin to sound charmingly old-fashioned.
examples.analytical: Shakespeare's witches are sometimes read through the figure of the grimalkin, a familiar animal that carried the suspicion of witchcraft.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a cat "Her Majesty" in a joke: it is a formal-sounding title for a plain animal.
nuance.etymology: From "Grey" (gray) plus "Malkin," an old name for a cat, probably from the name Maud or Matilda.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (GRIM-al-kin) instead of the second.
Using it as a neutral everyday word for any cat in casual speech.

senses.definition: Grayed, old.
Gray or partly gray.
Streaked or mixed with gray; grizzly; griseous.

core.definition: Having gray or partly gray hair, usually suggesting age and long experience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, reduce the second syllable to a schwa, and let the final d be a clean ending. The ld cluster is pronounced quickly, with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests experience, toughness and endurance, often in an older man.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use grizzled in descriptions of old veterans, detectives, coaches, farmers or ranchers, especially in the phrase 'grizzled veteran'. It is more descriptive and vivid than 'gray-haired', so it works well in stories, reviews and casual description. In everyday talk, 'he's got a grizzled beard' sounds natural.

distinctions.note: Gray-haired is the neutral, everyday description; grizzled adds a sense of ruggedness and experience.
Hoary is literary and can suggest great age or venerable dignity; grizzled is more rugged and less formal.
Salt-and-pepper describes hair mixing dark and gray in an informal way; grizzled suggests more weathered, older appearance.

examples.everyday: My grandpa has a grizzled beard and tells great stories.
examples.professional: We hired a grizzled engineer who has shipped three generations of firmware.
examples.analytical: The grizzled narrator embodies a world of worn loyalties, where age is measured less in years than in scars.

nuance.analogy: Like an old wooden fence weathered by many winters: gray, rough, and still standing.
nuance.etymology: From grizzle, 'gray', from Old French grisel, from gris, 'gray'.
common_mistakes: Confusing grizzled with grizzly: grizzled describes gray hair, while grizzly is the bear.
Using grizzled for a young person who has gray hair from stress; the word implies age and experience.

senses.definition: The mathematical theory of groups.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see group,‎ theory; a theory about (particular kinds of) groups.
senses.example: Her dissertation applied group theory to classify the symmetries of crystal lattices.

core.definition: The branch of mathematics that studies groups, which are sets with an operation that is associative, has an identity, and has inverses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress theory on the first syllable of the word, THEE, with the ending ree reduced to a light ee. The th is unvoiced, so place your tongue between your teeth.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term in mathematics and physics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use group theory in university mathematics, physics and cryptography. It refers to the abstract study of symmetry and structure, not to social groups. In casual talk, it is rarely used outside technical circles.

distinctions.note: Set theory studies collections of objects in general, while group theory studies sets with a specific algebraic operation.
A group in math is a structured set with an operation, not a collection of people.

examples.everyday: My son is studying group theory, so the homework is way over my head.
examples.professional: Our cryptography team uses group theory to choose secure parameters for the key exchange.
examples.analytical: Group theory reveals how symmetry constrains possible structures, which is why it explains so many physical laws.

nuance.analogy: Like a set of rotations of a square that can be combined, undone and kept in the same family.
nuance.etymology: Group comes from French groupe, from Italian gruppo; theory comes from Greek theōria, a looking at or contemplation.
common_mistakes: Confusing the mathematical group with a social group.
Using the plural groups theory; the phrase is normally singular.

senses.definition: The quality of readily believing information, truthful or otherwise, usually to an absurd extent.
senses.example: His gullibility made him the easy target of every online scam that landed in his inbox.

core.definition: A tendency to believe things too easily, even when they are false or unlikely; willingness to be fooled.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, BIL. The first vowel is a short u, as in 'cup', and the final -ity sounds like 'ih-tee' with a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a weakness, and saying someone has gullibility can sound critical or insulting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gullibility when talking about scams, advertising, or politics, for example 'the scam works because of people's gullibility.' In everyday talk people often say 'he will believe anything' instead. It is a serious word, so use it with care when speaking about a friend.

distinctions.note: Naivete describes a lack of experience or worldliness and can be affectionate; gullibility describes actually being fooled and is more critical.
Credulity is the more formal and technical word for believing too readily; gullibility is the everyday word.

examples.everyday: I can't believe you fell for that prize email; you have to watch your gullibility online.
examples.professional: Our phishing test showed that even experienced staff can display gullibility when a request appears to come from a manager.
examples.analytical: Gullibility is not simply stupidity; people often trust sources that look authoritative, which scammers deliberately exploit.

nuance.analogy: Gullibility is like a screen door with no latch: anything that knocks gets let in.
nuance.etymology: Derived from 'gullible' by adding the suffix '-ity'; 'gullible' comes from the Middle English-era verb 'gull', meaning to dupe.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle as 'guh-LIB-ih-lih-tee'; the stress is on BIL.
Confusing it with 'gullibleness', which is less common in American writing.

senses.definition: A writer of any of the Hagiographa․
Someone who writes the biography of a saint.
Someone who writes in an excessively flattering and laudatory way about a person (as if that person were a saint).

core.definition: A person who writes the lives of saints, or one who writes about someone in an overly flattering way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, AH. The g's are hard, as in 'go'. The ending -pher is a reduced 'fur', and the a in the stressed syllable is 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for a writer of saints' lives; negative when it implies uncritical, worshipful writing.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American writing the word is mostly used critically, as when a reviewer says a biographer is a hagiographer of a politician or CEO. In religious scholarship it is neutral. It is an educated word, rare in speech.

distinctions.note: A biographer writes about any life, ideally with balance; a hagiographer idealizes.
A sycophant flatters a person for gain; a hagiographer praises in writing, often sincerely.
An apologist defends a belief or person with arguments; a hagiographer celebrates with narrative.

collocations: a hagiographer rather than a historian

examples.everyday: That author is basically a hagiographer; he never mentions a single flaw.
examples.professional: The reviewer called the biographer a hagiographer, noting that the book ignored the founder's controversies.
examples.analytical: The early hagiographer shaped the saint's memory according to the conventions of the genre, not those of modern history.

nuance.analogy: A hagiographer paints with a halo brush: everything comes out glowing.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hagios, 'holy', plus -grapher, 'writer'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable: 'HAG-ee-og-ra-fer'.
Pronouncing the g as j: 'haj-ee'.
Using it as a neutral synonym for 'biographer'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hagiographa are the Writings, the third division of the Hebrew Bible (Ketuvim), including Psalms, Proverbs and Job. The word's older sense is a writer of one of these books.

senses.definition: To move or act in a quick fashion.
To make someone speed up or make something happen quicker.
To cause some scheduled event to happen earlier.

core.definition: To move or act more quickly, or to cause something to happen sooner than expected.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the final -en be a syllabic n with no separate vowel, so it sounds like 'HAY-sn.' Non-native speakers often add an extra 'eh' sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound a bit formal or literary compared with 'speed up' or 'hurry.'
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people usually say 'speed up,' 'hurry up,' or 'move things along.' Hasten shows up in writing, formal announcements, and speeches, such as 'We hope to hasten the process.' A natural reply to a formal announcement is simply 'That would be great.'

distinctions.note: Speed up is the everyday phrase for going faster, while hasten sounds more formal and often describes making an outcome arrive sooner.
Accelerate is common in technical and business writing about increasing speed or rate, while hasten suggests a more general or literary sense.

examples.everyday: Let's grab a taxi to hasten things along, because the movie starts at seven.
examples.professional: Automating the report generation should hasten our weekly reviews.
examples.analytical: Some theologians argue that human action cannot hasten the coming of the kingdom, which depends on God's own timing.

nuance.analogy: To hasten is like adding fuel to a fire: the flame does not change, but it grows and spreads faster.
nuance.etymology: From haste (noun), formed in Middle English from the noun haste.
common_mistakes: Using 'hasten' with a person as the object in casual speech, as in 'I hastened him,' which sounds stiff.
Pronouncing the final -en as a full syllable instead of a syllabic n.

senses.definition: Any of multiple lights fitted to the front and rear of a vehicle, used to warn other drivers of a dangerous situation, typically when the vehicle is not working properly.

core.definition: The flashing front and rear lights on a vehicle, switched on to warn other drivers of danger, especially when the car is stopped or broken down.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word on 'HAZ,' and the second word on 'LITES' with a strong primary stress. The 'ard' in 'hazard' reduces to a rhotic 'erd,' and 'lights' is a long i sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to serious; they signal a safety concern on the road.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'hazard lights' or 'hazards' in everyday speech, and the phrase is also used in driving instructions. Some people informally say 'flashers' or 'emergency flashers.' Use them when you are stopped on the shoulder, have a breakdown, or are driving very slowly in bad conditions.

distinctions.note: Turn signals show the direction you are turning or changing lanes; hazard lights warn that the vehicle itself is a danger.
Headlights help you see the road; hazard lights help other drivers see you.

examples.everyday: Put on your hazard lights so people know your car has broken down on the shoulder.
examples.professional: Our fleet policy requires drivers to switch on the hazard lights whenever a vehicle is stopped on the highway.
examples.analytical: The hazard lights communicate a warning without a specific direction, which is why they differ from turn signals in traffic law.

nuance.analogy: They work like a flashing sign that says 'careful, something is wrong here' to everyone behind you.
common_mistakes: Saying 'emergency lights' or 'flash lights' as the standard name; Americans usually say 'hazard lights.'
Using 'hazard lights' to signal a turn; that job belongs to the turn signal.

senses.definition: One who makes or mends hedges.
senses.example: Our neighbor is a skilled hedger who trims the boxwood every autumn.

senses.definition: One who hedges, for example in betting.
senses.example: A savvy hedger bet against his own team to limit his losses.

core.definition: A person who reduces financial risk by taking an offsetting position in a market, or a person who avoids committing to a clear position.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The g is pronounced like j, and the final -er is a light, unstressed American r-sound, not 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in finance, where hedgers are a normal part of markets. Negative when describing a person who will not commit to a view in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, the financial sense is common in business news, especially for commodities such as oil, corn, and currencies. Airlines and farm cooperatives are often described as hedgers. In everyday talk, calling someone a hedger suggests they avoid taking a stand, so it can sound like criticism.

distinctions.note: A hedger takes a position to reduce an existing risk, while a speculator takes on risk in hopes of profit.
A hedger is usually a company protecting its own business exposure, while a hedge fund manager invests pooled money for clients, often with speculative strategies.

examples.everyday: My brother is a hedger in his job, so he's always careful about what he says before he commits to anything.
examples.professional: As a commodity hedger, our company buys futures contracts to lock in fuel prices for the next year.
examples.analytical: The political commentator is a chronic hedger, never endorsing a position without qualifying it into meaninglessness.

nuance.analogy: A hedger is like someone who buys a roof rain insurance policy for a picnic: the action reduces possible damage without changing the weather.
nuance.etymology: Agent noun from the verb hedge, which comes from Old English hecg, meaning a barrier or enclosure.
common_mistakes: Saying the g as a hard /g/ sound instead of the j sound in /dʒ/.
Using hedger for anyone who simply says 'maybe'; the word usually refers to a person who systematically avoids commitment or to someone managing financial risk.

senses.definition: The cry of an ass or donkey.
senses.example: Hee-haw! shouted the kids, imitating the donkey at the petting zoo.

senses.definition: Nothing.
senses.example: After all that promising, the company delivered hee-haw for its investors this quarter.

senses.definition: The cry of an ass or donkey.
senses.example: Hee-haw! shouted the kids, imitating the donkey at the petting zoo.

senses.definition: Of an ass or donkey, to make its typical vocalisation.
senses.example: At dawn the donkey began to hee-haw loudly outside our bedroom window.

senses.definition: To mimic the cry of an ass or donkey; to make a noise resembling a donkey's vocalisations.
senses.example: The comedian would hee-haw into the microphone to imitate a stubborn mule.

core.definition: The loud, harsh braying sound made by a donkey or ass.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HEE. The second syllable is an open 'hah', not the 'how' sound of 'hour'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful. It is often used in children's stories, jokes, and imitations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hee-haw mainly for the donkey's sound, especially in children's books, farm talk, and jokes. It is a playful, imitative word, so it is best in casual speech rather than formal writing. Many Americans first learned it from the TV variety show Hee Haw, a long-running country music comedy program. For a more general or technical term, say bray.

distinctions.note: Bray is the standard word for a donkey's cry, while hee-haw is more imitative and childlike.
Neigh is the sound a horse makes, while hee-haw is specifically the donkey's sound.

collocations: the donkey let out a hee-haw

examples.everyday: Did you hear that donkey hee-haw at the petting zoo? The kids started laughing right away.
examples.professional: In the picture book manuscript, the donkey's line should read hee-haw, since young readers repeat it.
examples.analytical: The onomatopoeic hee-haw imitates the donkey's rhythmic cry, which is why the sound is so easily recognized across English.

nuance.analogy: A hee-haw is like a sound effect in a cartoon: it is instantly recognizable because it copies the real noise.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of the donkey's bray.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing haw as 'how', when the American sound is more like 'hah'.
Writing hee haw without a hyphen in formal writing, since the hyphenated form is standard.

senses.definition: The part of a shoe's sole which supports the foot's heel.
The rear part of a sock or similar covering for the foot.
The part of the palm of a hand closest to the wrist.
senses.example: He drove the heel of his hand into the man's nose.

senses.definition: A high-heeled shoe.
senses.example: She wore red high heels to the office party, though her feet hurt by nine.

senses.definition: The back, upper part of the stock.
senses.example: The rifle's heel pressed hard against my shoulder when I fired the shotgun.

senses.definition: The last or lowest part of anything.
senses.example: the heel of a mast

senses.definition: The base of a bun sliced in half lengthwise.
senses.example: The burger was good, but the heel of the bun was soggy from the ketchup.

senses.definition: A contemptible, unscrupulous, inconsiderate, or thoughtless person.
senses.example: Dan is a heel who skipped his own sister's wedding without any explanation.

senses.definition: A headlining wrestler regarded as a "bad guy," whose ring persona embodies villainous or reprehensible traits and demonstrates characteristics of a braggart and a bully.
senses.example: The crowd booed loudly every time the heel strutted into the ring to taunt the champion.

senses.definition: The cards set aside for later use in a patience or solitaire game.
senses.example: Before she could finish the game, she had to move the heel cards back into play.

senses.definition: Anything resembling a human heel in shape; a protuberance; a knob.
senses.example: A small heel of rock jutted out from the cliff, perfect for a bird to perch.

senses.definition: The obtuse angle of the lower end of a rafter set sloping.
senses.example: The carpenter marked the heel of each rafter where it rests on the top plate.

senses.definition: The short side of an angled cut.
senses.example: Measure from the heel of the miter cut to get the exact length of the board.

senses.definition: The part of a club head's face nearest the shaft.
senses.example: Her drive went wrong when she hit the ball off the heel of the driver.

senses.definition: The lower end of the bit (cutting edge) of an axehead, as opposed to the toe (upper end).
senses.example: Keep the bit of the axe sharp, especially near the heel where it does most of the chopping.

senses.definition: The part of a carding machine's flat nearest the cylinder.
senses.example: The wire teeth near the heel of the flat wore down faster than the rest.
