senses.example: Without someone to supervise them, the group will lack direction.

senses.definition: To oversee a task, organization, etc. to provide supervision; to act as a supervisor.
senses.example: The senior nurse will supervise the new staff during their first two weeks.

core.definition: To watch over and direct the work of others, making sure that tasks are done correctly and on time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SOO. The middle syllable is a weak r-vowel, and the final -ise is pronounced like 'eyes' with a z sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word describes a job or role; it can sound controlling when used of a manager who watches too closely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use supervise for the daily oversight of employees, students, interns, or construction work. In an office you might say 'Who supervises you?' For a more casual idea, Americans often say 'oversee' or 'be in charge of'. Supervise is also used in academia: a professor supervises a dissertation. In everyday talk, 'watch' or 'keep an eye on' is more natural for children or pets.

distinctions.note: Oversee is broader and more general, covering a whole project from above; supervise suggests direct, hands-on watching of the people doing the work.
Manage covers planning, budgets and results; supervise focuses on the daily work and workers being watched.

examples.everyday: My sister supervises the night shift at a bakery, so she's always up early.
examples.professional: I supervise two data engineers, so please send your questions about the pipeline to me or to them directly.
examples.analytical: A good academic institution must balance the freedom of scholars with the duty to supervise their research ethically.

nuance.analogy: Like a lifeguard on a crowded beach, watching the swimmers so the work stays safe and on track.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin supervisus, past participle of supervidere 'to oversee', from super 'over' and videre 'to see'.
common_mistakes: Adding a preposition: say 'supervise the team', not 'supervise over the team'.
Stressing the second syllable (su-PER-vise); the stress is on SOO.

senses.definition: Initialism of singular value decomposition.

core.definition: Singular value decomposition: a factorization of a matrix into three matrices, used in data analysis and dimensionality reduction.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters S, V and D separately, with the stress on the last letter, DEE. Learners often stress the first letter or run the three letters together as one word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and purely technical, used in mathematics, statistics and machine learning.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and engineers say the letters one at a time, ess-vee-dee, and usually write SVD in papers and code. In casual talk you would say matrix factorization or just the decomposition. When you explain it, name the matrix, since the same initials can mean other things in different fields.

distinctions.note: Principal component analysis is closely related: PCA is often computed using the SVD of the centered data matrix, so PCA is the method and SVD is the matrix tool.
Eigendecomposition applies only to square matrices, while SVD works for any rectangular matrix.

examples.everyday: My friend who does machine learning said her recommendation system uses SVD under the hood.
examples.professional: Let's run SVD on the user-item matrix to reduce the feature count before we train the model.
examples.analytical: The proof shows that every real matrix admits an SVD, which yields the best low-rank approximation in the Frobenius norm.

nuance.analogy: Like breaking a song into its basic notes and the loudness of each, so you can rebuild it or drop the quiet parts.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of singular value decomposition; singular comes from Latin singularis, 'single'.
common_mistakes: Saying it as one word, like sahv or svid; say the letters separately.
Stressing the first letter instead of the last: ess-vee-DEE.

senses.definition: One who swings.
A person who practices swinging (sex with different partners).
A bet in which the bettor must correctly pick two runners to finish in any of the places in any order.
senses.example: My uncle always places a swinger on the Saturday races, picking two horses to finish in the top three.

senses.definition: A performer of swing music or whose style is influenced by swing.
senses.example: The swinger played clarinet in a sixties-style band that revived big band tunes at the club.

senses.definition: A swing voter.
A swing ride.
A passenger on a motorcycle's sidecar who athletically moves from one side to the other to alter the weight distribution.
senses.example: The sidecar swinger shifted his weight across the bike at every sharp turn on the mountain road.

senses.definition: One who swinges.

core.definition: A person or thing that swings, such as a batter or golfer; in slang, someone who swaps sexual partners with others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -er is a light, reduced syllable with an American r, not a full 'air' sound. Keep the ng without adding a g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in sports and everyday uses; the sexual slang sense is informal and can sound suggestive, so it depends on context.
nuance.usage_note: In sports talk, a 'big swinger' is a powerful hitter, and it is a neutral, casual term. The sexual meaning is slang, referring to couples who exchange partners, and it is not used in polite company without context. If you mean a dancer, say swing dancer.

distinctions.note: A swing dancer performs the swing dance style; a swinger on its own can be misread, so use the full term for dance.
Polyamorous describes ongoing relationships with several partners; swinging usually refers to casual sex with other couples.

collocations: a good swinger of the bat

examples.everyday: Stand back during batting practice, because he's a big swinger.
examples.professional: The coach picked a left-handed swinger to face the right-handed pitcher in the ninth inning.
examples.analytical: Early baseball writers called every power hitter a swinger, a label that shows how the game prized a bold, full swing.

nuance.analogy: A swinger is like a gate on a hinge: the force comes from one side, and the motion is a full arc.
nuance.etymology: From swing (verb) with the agent suffix -er, meaning one who swings.
common_mistakes: Using swinger in a polite conversation for the sexual sense without context; in everyday talk it can be misunderstood.
Assuming swinger means a dancer; for dancers Americans say swing dancer.

senses.definition: Tending to swoon (in any sense).

core.definition: Tending to swoon; feeling or causing dreamy, lovestruck admiration, or feeling faint with excitement or emotion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the oo is a long vowel like in soon. The final -y is a clear ee sound, not ih.

nuance.connotation: Positive or playful; it describes romantic gushiness or a dreamy effect, often with a bit of teasing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use swoony mostly in casual speech and writing, especially about romance, celebrities, movies, or a sweet gesture from a partner. It is friendly and lighthearted, but it can sound silly in a serious or professional setting. A natural reply to a swoony remark is a laugh or an agreement like Right? I know.

distinctions.note: Romantic describes love or a love-related quality in general, while swoony suggests a more giddy, breathless, gushing reaction.
Dreamy can describe a person's looks or a soft, pleasant atmosphere, while swoony focuses on the feeling of being overwhelmed with delight.

examples.everyday: He surprised her with breakfast in bed and a handwritten note, which is so swoony.
examples.professional: The marketing team's swoony slogan tested well with focus groups, but legal wanted something more precise.
examples.analytical: Critics often dismiss romantic fiction as swoony, but such texts can teach readers about desire and vulnerability.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden rush of warm feeling that makes your knees go weak, swoony describes a reaction that is light and overwhelming at once.
nuance.etymology: Formed from swoon (to faint) plus the suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using swoony for a physical faint, when it usually means romantic or emotional delight.
Pronouncing the oo as in foot instead of the long vowel in soon.

senses.definition: To combine different elements, or to unite or reconcile different beliefs.
To merge different inflexional forms.

core.definition: To combine different religious beliefs, practices or cultural elements into one system, often blending them together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SING, and the middle syllable is a reduced schwa. The -ize ending sounds like 'ize' in 'eyes', not 'eez'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly critical. In scholarship it is descriptive; in religious debates it can suggest mixing things that should stay separate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'syncretize' mostly in academic writing and religious studies. In conversation they say 'blend' or 'combine'. Choose this verb when you want to describe how two traditions fused over time, not when you simply put two things side by side.

distinctions.note: Synthesize means combining ideas into a new whole, while syncretize often refers to blending religions or cultures, sometimes without resolving contradictions.
Assimilate means one group absorbs into another's culture, while syncretize describes a mixture in which both sides contribute.

examples.everyday: Over the years, my in-laws have syncretized their church rituals with old family customs from the village.
examples.professional: In our church-planting team meeting, we discussed how new believers sometimes syncretize local customs with their new faith.
examples.analytical: Historians argue that medieval Christians often syncretized pagan festivals with feasts of the saints, creating hybrid calendars.

nuance.analogy: Like cooks merging two family recipes into one dish, a community syncretizes two traditions into a new practice.
nuance.etymology: From syncretism, from Greek synkretismos, 'union of Cretans'.
common_mistakes: Using 'syncretize' for simply mixing ingredients or everyday objects; it is for beliefs and cultures.
Confusing 'syncretize' with 'synchronize' because they sound similar.

senses.definition: A tableau (group scene resembling a painting).

core.definition: A silent, motionless group scene in which living people pose like a painting or sculpture, often as entertainment.

pronunciation.tip: This is a French phrase, but Americans stress BLOH in the first word and VAHNT in the second. Do not say 'vee-VON' with a French nasal vowel; use a clear American 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it suggests art, theater or a deliberate, staged moment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mainly in theater, art history, museum education and discussions of historical entertainment. It is rarely used in casual speech. The plural is tableaux vivants, though tableaux vivant is also seen in English writing.

distinctions.note: A tableau is any group arrangement or dramatic scene, including a painting; a tableau vivant specifically means living people posing silently.
A still life depicts inanimate objects such as fruit or flowers; a tableau vivant uses people as the figures in the frozen scene.

collocations: a tableau vivant at the party

examples.everyday: Our church youth group did a tableau vivant of the nativity scene for the Christmas party.
examples.professional: The museum education team staged a tableau vivant to help visitors see how the painting was composed.
examples.analytical: The novel's climax is a tableau vivant in which the characters freeze in silence, turning spectacle into judgment.

nuance.analogy: A tableau vivant is like pausing a movie on one frame and asking living people to become that frame.
nuance.etymology: French, meaning 'living picture'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing vivant with a French nasal vowel rather than an American 'vih-VAHNT'.
Dropping the second word or saying 'living tableau', which is understood but less standard in formal writing.

senses.definition: Having no tact; unaware or intentionally inconsiderate of someone else's feelings.
senses.example: It was tactless of you not to attend your sister's wedding.

core.definition: Saying or doing things that hurt or embarrass people because one does not think about their feelings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the 'ct' clearly. The final syllable is a reduced 'us' sound, not 'ess.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes someone for hurting others by careless speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tactless to describe a remark or person who said something hurtful without thinking, such as 'That was tactless of him to bring up her divorce.' It is common in everyday conversation and in workplace feedback. Calling someone tactless directly can be harsh, so people often soften it with 'a bit tactless.'

distinctions.note: Rude means deliberately impolite; tactless means careless about feelings, often without intending harm.
Blunt describes honest, direct speech; tactless describes speech that ignores how it will affect the listener.

examples.everyday: That was a tactless thing to say at the funeral, honestly.
examples.professional: Asking the candidate about her age in the interview was tactless and could create legal problems.
examples.analytical: The narrator's tactless honesty exposes the gap between truthfulness and kindness.

nuance.analogy: A tactless remark is like stepping on someone's toe while trying to reach for the door: you did not mean to hurt them, but you did.
nuance.etymology: From tact plus the suffix -less, meaning 'without.'
common_mistakes: Using tactless to mean 'dishonest'; it describes a lack of sensitivity, not a lack of truthfulness.
Using 'tactless' for 'impolite' in a deliberate insult, where 'rude' is more accurate.
patterns: it was tactless (of sb) to do sth

core.definition: A Levite of the Kohathite line, named among the ancestors in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, linked to the family of the temple musicians.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the 'th' at the end as in 'bath.' Don't add an extra vowel after the 'h.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a name in Scripture with no evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Tahath is a biblical name used mainly in Bible study, scholarly discussion, and church reading. Americans would not use it in everyday conversation. Readers often encounter it in genealogy lists, where they can skip it without losing the thread.

distinctions.note: Tahath is a person's name in the genealogies, while Tahpanhes is a city in Egypt.

examples.everyday: In the Bible study group, someone asked who Tahath was, and we found him in the genealogy of Levi.
examples.professional: In the commentary on 1 Chronicles, Tahath is treated as one name in the Kohathite line of Levitical ancestors.
examples.analytical: The genealogical lists of Tahath reflect the effort to preserve Levitical lineage for temple service.

nuance.analogy: Tahath is like a name on a family tree that shows how one branch connects to another.
common_mistakes: Confusing Tahath with Tahpanhes, which is a city.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Tahath appears as a Levite of the Kohathite family in the genealogies, which trace the lineage of temple service. He is named in 1 Chronicles 6:24 among the descendants of Kohath, and another Tahath, an Ephraimite, is named in 1 Chronicles 7:20. In these passages the name serves to record family lines rather than to tell a narrative about Tahath himself.

senses.definition: To go for a walk.
To go away, get lost.
(dated) To leave; to quit.
senses.example: Hear the sound of that? It's the sound of me taking a walk.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To go out for a walk; informally, to go away, often rudely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'walk', and the l is silent. Many Americans say the vowel like 'caught', while others say it like 'wok'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the literal sense; negative and rude for the slang sense of 'go away'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say 'Let's take a walk' for a relaxed stroll after dinner or a break at work. The slang sense, 'Take a walk!', is rude and used in anger, much like 'take a hike.' The old sense of 'to quit' is rarely heard in American speech. A natural reply to the literal sense is 'Sounds good.'

distinctions.note: 'Go for a walk' is the most common everyday phrase in American speech and is more standard than 'take a walk'.
'Stroll' describes a slow, relaxed walk, while 'take a walk' is a general term for any walk.
'Take a hike' is the rude sense 'go away' and can also mean a literal hike; 'take a walk' is more often a gentle stroll.

collocations: take a walk in the park
take a walk around the block

examples.everyday: I need a break, so I'm going to take a walk around the block.
examples.professional: Let's take a walk to the conference room and talk through the deadline in person.
examples.analytical: Many writers describe taking a walk as a way to let ideas settle before they commit an argument to paper.

nuance.analogy: Like pressing a reset button for the mind.
common_mistakes: Using 'take a walk' for a long, demanding trek; 'hike' is the better word for that.
Saying 'go walk' or 'take walk' without the article 'a'; the natural form is 'go for a walk' or 'take a walk'.

senses.definition: Discuss something later, outside the meeting, with fewer people.

core.definition: To move a discussion out of the current meeting to a later, smaller conversation.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on OFF, with secondary stress on LINE. Note that 'offline' is pronounced with a full ow-like vowel, not 'off-lyn', and the t in 'it' is often a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces, especially tech companies, this phrase is used when a debate is taking too long or includes too many people. A typical reply is 'Sure, let's sync after the meeting.' It can sound slightly managerial, so use it politely.

distinctions.vs: take it up after the meeting
distinctions.note: Both mean discuss later; 'take it offline' is more jargon-heavy and common in tech.
'Table it' means postpone without a set time; 'take it offline' implies a separate follow-up conversation.

examples.everyday: We're arguing about dinner plans in front of everyone, so let's take it offline later.
examples.professional: This debate about the API design is taking too long, so let's take it offline and include only the owners.
examples.analytical: Rather than settle the dispute in plenary, the committee chose to take it offline to a smaller working group.

nuance.analogy: Like moving a loud argument from the living room into the kitchen with only the people who need to be there.
common_mistakes: Using 'offline' only as 'not connected to the internet'; in meetings it means outside the meeting.
Saying 'take it off-line' with a hyphen in speech, which is unnatural.

conversation.text: This is getting into the details. Can we take it offline?
Let's take it offline so we don't hold up the whole group.
James and I will take it offline and report back.

senses.definition: To discuss; to converse about a matter or issue.
senses.example: Come home early, we have a lot to talk over.

senses.definition: To verbally interrupt (someone); to speak at the same time as someone else.
senses.example: She rudely talked over her opponent in the debate.

senses.definition: To persuade (someone); to talk around.
senses.example: I didn't like the idea at first, but they eventually talked me over.

core.definition: To discuss a matter with someone, especially to reach a decision; also, to interrupt someone by speaking while they are still talking.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle 'over' (OH-ver), and say the final syllable as a reduced American 'er', not 'ow-ver'. The 'v' is voiced, linking smoothly to the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when meaning 'discuss'; negative when meaning 'interrupt' or 'drown out', because it suggests someone is not being listened to.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, 'let's talk it over' is a common, friendly way to suggest discussing a problem before deciding. The sense 'talk over someone' means to keep speaking while someone else is trying to talk, and Americans often find this rude, especially in meetings. Context makes the meaning clear.

distinctions.note: 'Discuss' is more formal and direct; 'talk over' is casual and often implies a personal, relaxed conversation about a decision.
'Interrupt' means breaking in; 'talk over' specifically means continuing to speak loudly while another person is speaking.

examples.everyday: Let's talk it over tonight and decide whether we should move closer to your parents.
examples.professional: Can we talk over the migration plan with the infrastructure team before we send the change request?
examples.analytical: Hobbes suggests that when people talk over one another in public debate, reasoned argument gives way to the loudest voice.

nuance.analogy: Like two people passing a ball of ideas back and forth until they settle on one.
nuance.etymology: From 'talk' plus 'over', meaning across or through a matter, from Old English ofer.
common_mistakes: Using 'talk over' for a simple 'talk about' in formal writing, where 'discuss' is more natural.
Forgetting that 'talk over someone' is rude in American meetings; it is better to say 'Sorry, go ahead' or 'Can I finish?'

conversation.text: Let's talk it over at lunch tomorrow.
We talked over the offer before I accepted it.
Stop talking over me; let me finish.

senses.definition: Someone who supervises workers, especially one who imposes hard or burdensome work.
A source of hard work or responsibility.
Someone who is capable of performing many tasks; a multitasker.

core.definition: A person who demands hard work from others, often in a strict or harsh way, or who pushes others to complete difficult tasks.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -er is a reduced American r sound. Keep the secondary stress light on master.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests someone who is strict, demanding or harsh, though it can be used more lightly for a coach or manager.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use taskmaster for bosses, coaches or parents who push people hard. It can be half-joking, as in 'My trainer is a real taskmaster.' It is usually not a compliment unless the speaker wants to praise discipline. In a workplace, describing someone as a taskmaster can suggest that they are demanding but effective.

distinctions.note: Boss is a general word for a supervisor, while taskmaster specifically highlights demanding, strict control over work.
Supervisor is neutral and formal, while taskmaster carries a strong sense of pressure and hardship.

examples.everyday: My gym coach is a real taskmaster, but I feel stronger every week.
examples.professional: Our manager is a taskmaster about deadlines, so the team always delivers on time.
examples.analytical: The author describes the economy as a taskmaster that drives people past their natural limits.

nuance.analogy: A taskmaster is like a coach with a whistle who never lets the team rest.
nuance.etymology: From task plus master, meaning one who sets and enforces tasks.
common_mistakes: Using taskmaster for a friendly teacher without the sense of pressure.
Writing it as two words, task master, in formal writing where the single compound is standard.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Old Testament, taskmasters are the Egyptian overseers who forced the Israelites to do hard labor. The Hebrew word is nogesh, meaning an overseer or driver of workers. Exodus 1:11 says Egypt set taskmasters over Israel to afflict them with burdens, and Exodus 3:7 describes God hearing the cry of his people because of their taskmasters. Exodus 5:6 shows Pharaoh ordering the taskmasters to stop giving straw to the people.

senses.definition: To rend (a solid material) by holding or restraining in two places and pulling apart, whether intentionally or not; to destroy or separate.
senses.example: He tore his coat on the nail.

senses.definition: To injure as if by pulling apart.
senses.example: He tore some muscles in a weight-lifting accident.

senses.definition: To destroy or reduce abstract unity or coherence, such as social, political or emotional.
senses.example: He was torn by conflicting emotions.

senses.definition: To make (an opening) with force or energy.
senses.example: A piece of debris tore a tiny straight channel through the satellite.

senses.definition: To remove by tearing, or with sudden great force.
senses.example: Tear the coupon out of the newspaper.

senses.definition: To demolish.
senses.example: The slums were torn down to make way for the new development.

senses.definition: To become torn, especially accidentally.
senses.example: My dress has torn.

senses.definition: To move or act with great speed, energy, or violence.
senses.example: He went tearing down the hill at 90 miles per hour.

senses.definition: To smash or enter something with great force.
senses.example: The chain shot tore into the approaching line of infantry.

senses.definition: To be interrupted midway through.
senses.example: torn write

senses.definition: To produce tears.
senses.example: Her eyes began to tear in the harsh wind.

senses.definition: A hole or break caused by tearing.
senses.example: A small tear is easy to mend, if it is on the seam.

senses.definition: A rampage.
senses.example: to go on a tear

senses.definition: A drop of clear, salty liquid produced from the eyes by crying or irritation.
senses.example: Big tears streamed from Lisa's eyes, rolling down her cheeks.

senses.definition: Something in the form of a transparent drop of fluid matter; also, a solid, transparent, tear-shaped drop, as of some balsams or resins.
senses.example: A single tear rolled down her cheek as the anthem ended.

senses.definition: A partially vitrified bit of clay in glass.
senses.example: The glassblower discarded the piece because a tear of unmelted clay was visible inside.

senses.definition: That which causes or accompanies tears; a lament; a dirge.
senses.example: Her poem was a tear for the lost fishing towns of her childhood.

core.definition: To pull something apart by force, making a hole, break or split in it, either on purpose or by accident.

pronunciation.tip: For the rip sense, the vowel rhymes with 'air' and 'hair'. The crying noun is different: it is pronounced /tɪɹ/, rhyming with 'here'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes damage or physical separation and can be negative when it means injury or destruction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tear for paper, cloth, skin and emotional situations, and it appears often in everyday talk: 'Don't tear the page' or 'I tore my jeans on the fence.' For the crying sense, the noun is pronounced 'teer' and is often used in phrases such as 'tears of joy'. The noun meaning a hole or break is pronounced 'tair'.

distinctions.note: Rip is more sudden and uneven, often used for clothing or paper; tear is the more general word and can also mean a physical or emotional split.
Cut suggests a clean separation made with a sharp tool; tear suggests pulling a material apart, often leaving a rough edge.

examples.everyday: Be careful opening that box, you'll tear the cardboard if you rush.
examples.professional: Please don't tear the printouts apart; the audit team needs the original copies.
examples.analytical: Any argument that tries to reconcile these texts will tear the apparent contradiction open rather than hide it.

nuance.analogy: Tearing is like pulling a loaf of bread apart: the force follows the weakest line and leaves a ragged edge.
nuance.etymology: From Old English teran, to rend or tear apart.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the rip verb and the crying noun the same way; the crying noun rhymes with 'here'.
Using 'tear' as a noun when the rip sense is intended; 'a tear' means a hole, and 'tear' as an action is a verb.

tear.etymology: From Middle English *teren*, from Old English *teran* (“to tear, lacerate”), from Proto-Germanic **teraną* (“to tear, tear apart, rip”), from Proto-Indo-European **der-* (“to tear, tear apart”).

senses.definition: To function as a liability (for someone); to put into a condition of disadvantage.
senses.example: Her early mistake told against her when she applied for the promotion.

senses.definition: To serve as evidence which casts doubt upon.
senses.example: The missing receipt told against the claim that the payment was made on time.

core.definition: To count against someone or something, hurting their chances or serving as evidence that weakens their case.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'gen' in 'against', with 'tell' lightly stressed. The 'ag' vowel is a reduced 'uh', and the final 'st' is clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It always describes something that hurts a person or case.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tell against' mainly in news, legal, sports and academic writing, and occasionally in careful speech. In everyday talk they usually say 'work against you' or 'hurt your chances'. A natural reply might be 'That's a fair point, so I'll fix it.'

distinctions.note: 'Count against' is more everyday and is used for a factor that reduces a person's chances; 'tell against' sounds more like evidence.
'Work against' is more casual and suggests an active obstacle, while 'tell against' often implies evidence or impression.
'Tell for' means supporting or favoring someone, the opposite of 'tell against'.

examples.everyday: Showing up late to the interview might tell against you, so set an alarm tomorrow.
examples.professional: The missed deadline will tell against the team in next quarter's performance review.
examples.analytical: The contradictory testimony tells against the witness's credibility, though it does not by itself prove that he lied.

nuance.analogy: It works like a heavy weight on a scale, pulling the result in the wrong direction.
nuance.etymology: Combines 'tell' (from Old English tellan 'count') with 'against'; the phrasal sense is an English idiom.
common_mistakes: Using 'tell against' to mean supporting evidence; it always means negative evidence.
Confusing it with 'tell on', which means to inform on someone.

senses.definition: Reckless boldness; foolish bravery.
An act or case of reckless boldness.
Effrontery; impudence.
senses.example: She had the temerity to ask for a raise on her first day of work.

core.definition: Reckless boldness, or the nerve to do something risky or rude without regard for consequences, often in a way that seems disrespectful.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MEH, and the first syllable is a weak schwa. The final -ity is usually a soft 'tee' or a flapped 'dee' in fast speech, not a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that someone was bold in a way others found presumptuous or foolish, though it can sound admiring in a wry way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use temerity mostly in writing, news commentary, and formal speech, rather than in casual conversation. You might hear someone say he had the temerity to do something when they are annoyed. The everyday American equivalent is nerve or gall, as in he had the nerve to ask for a raise.

distinctions.note: Audacity can be admired as daring and creative, while temerity usually suggests recklessness or disrespect.
Nerve is informal and everyday, and it often describes courage in a tense moment; temerity is more formal and always carries some criticism.
Courage is a moral strength aimed at a good end, while temerity is boldness that is careless about danger or others' feelings.

examples.everyday: He had the temerity to ask my sister for a loan on their first date.
examples.professional: It took real temerity to propose cutting the pilot before we had any results.
examples.analytical: Critics of the argument questioned the temerity of claiming certainty about causes that experience can never fully confirm.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who speeds through a red light because he assumes no one will stop him, temerity is confidence that ignores the real risk.
nuance.etymology: From Latin temeritas, meaning rashness or chance, from temere, meaning blindly or by chance.
common_mistakes: Using temerity as a synonym for courage in a positive sense; it usually criticizes the boldness.
Stressing the first syllable (TEM-uh-ruh-tee) instead of the second.
patterns: [U] have the temerity to do sth

temerity.etymology: From Middle English *temerite*, *temeryte*, from Old French *temerité*, from Latin *temeritās* (“chance, accident, rashness”), from *temere* (“by chance, casually, rashly”).

senses.definition: In a tenuous manner.

core.definition: In a weak, fragile, or uncertain way; with only a slight or doubtful basis, connection, or support.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ous is reduced to a quick us, not oos, and the -ly ending is a light lee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It usually signals doubt or weakness in a claim, link, or plan.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tenuously mostly in formal writing, news analysis, academic work, and business reports, where it describes a link that is weak or fragile. In casual speech they say 'barely', 'loosely', or 'by a thread'. Using tenuously in conversation can sound stiff but is not rude.

distinctions.note: Precariously stresses danger of falling or failing; tenuously stresses that the connection itself is weak.
Loosely is casual and general; tenuously is more formal and suggests the link is thin or doubtful.

examples.everyday: My job is only tenuously connected to my degree, but it pays the bills.
examples.professional: The chart shows that the two metrics are only tenuously correlated, so we should not forecast from it.
examples.analytical: The argument rests tenuously on a single contested premise about human nature.

nuance.analogy: Like a kite held by a single thin thread: it is up there, but any gust could break the link.
nuance.etymology: From tenuous, from Latin tenuis 'thin', with the adverbial -ly.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as tenously or tenuosly.
Saying TEN-yoo-ous with an extra syllable.
Using tenuously in casual talk where 'barely' would be more natural.

senses.definition: The property of being thankless.

core.definition: The quality of being thankless; work or effort that receives little or no gratitude or recognition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The -ness ending is a reduced 'nus', so keep it short and do not insert an extra vowel between the k and the l.

nuance.connotation: Negative and sympathetic, describing an unrewarded situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use thanklessness in everyday speech. They usually say a thankless job or the thankless nature of the work. You will see it more often in essays, reviews, or op-eds about overlooked labor.

distinctions.note: Ingratitude is a failure of a person to be grateful; thanklessness is the situation of receiving no gratitude for one's work.
Thankless is the adjective used in most sentences; thanklessness is the noun for talking about the quality itself.

examples.professional: We need to address the thanklessness of on-call rotations, or we will lose our best engineers.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the thanklessness of domestic labor is a moral problem, not merely a personal disappointment.

nuance.analogy: Like a tree that gives shade to everyone and never hears who thanked it.
nuance.etymology: From thankless plus the suffix -ness, meaning 'state or quality of'.
common_mistakes: Using it in casual speech, where 'a thankless job' sounds more natural.
Pronouncing the last syllable with a long e, as in 'THANK-lus-nees'.
Confusing it with ingratitude, which describes a person's attitude rather than a situation.

senses.definition: Used as an intensifier.
senses.example: Why the dickens did he do that?

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see the,‎ dickens; the devil.
senses.example: She can go to the dickens for what she said.

core.definition: A mild, old-fashioned intensifier in questions, meaning 'the devil,' used to express surprise or irritation, as in 'What the dickens happened?'

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DIK, and the second syllable is a weak uhn. The final s is a voiced z sound, and the word is an old euphemism.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful. It sounds mild and slightly old-fashioned, so it can add a light, folksy tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this as a polite substitute for 'the devil' or 'the hell' in questions, as in 'What the dickens?' It is heard mostly from older speakers, in folksy storytelling, and in children's books, and it can sound quaint to younger people. A natural reply is an answer, or 'Beats me.'

distinctions.note: The devil is a little stronger and more emphatic, while the dickens is a gentler euphemism.
The heck is more common today and equally mild; the dickens sounds more old-fashioned.

examples.everyday: What the dickens happened to the Wi-Fi? It keeps cutting out.
examples.professional: How the dickens did we miss the deadline when the calendar said we had two weeks?
examples.analytical: Why the dickens a model trained on clean data should fail so badly on noisy inputs is the question the robustness literature keeps returning to.

nuance.analogy: Like a costume for a swear word: the same shape, but a gentler look.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; probably a euphemism for 'devil' used in mild oaths.
common_mistakes: Using the dickens in formal writing as if it were a serious term; it is playful and dated.
Pronouncing the final s as a sharp s; it is a voiced z sound.

senses.definition: Partaking of, or combining, both divinity and humanity.

core.definition: Combining both divine and human nature or qualities in one being.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on the -throp- syllable, with weaker stress on the first syllable. Both 'th' sounds are voiceless, and the final -ic is short /ɪk/, not /aɪk/.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a specialized theological term that is not used in ordinary talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mainly in theology, seminary study, and Eastern Orthodox writing about Christ's union of God and man. You may also see it in literary writing about hybrid or mythic beings. In everyday speech, say 'fully divine and fully human' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Divine' describes only God, while 'theanthropic' stresses the union of God and humanity in one being.
'Incarnate' means embodied in flesh and can be used loosely for ideas or qualities, while 'theanthropic' is a precise technical term about two natures.

examples.everyday: My priest said the Incarnation is a theanthropic mystery, so I'm still trying to wrap my head around it.
examples.professional: In the seminary lecture, the professor described Christ's theanthropic person as the foundation for the doctrine of salvation.
examples.analytical: Maximus the Confessor's account of the theanthropic union preserves both the full divinity and the full humanity of Christ without confusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a coin that is both metal and money at once, one object with two natures.
nuance.etymology: From Greek theos (god) and anthrōpos (human being).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'anthropic' (relating to human existence in cosmology); the prefix 'thea-' is what makes it theological.
Stressing the 'an' syllable; the primary stress is on '-throp-'.

senses.definition: A person who has a personal knowledge of God through prayer, asceticism, and mystical experience.
A specialist in academic theology.
Someone who studies theology.
senses.example: Seminarians are usually divided into philosophers and theologians, depending on their stage of formation.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) A theological lecturer attached to a cathedral church.

core.definition: A person who studies or writes about God and religious beliefs, usually as a trained scholar or teacher of theology.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOH, and the -gian ending is a reduced schwa plus n, so it sounds like 'jun,' not 'gee-an.' The first syllable can sound like 'thee-uh' in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a respected scholar or a trained expert, though some believers may use the word more loosely for any thoughtful person who writes about faith.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use theologian for professors at seminaries and divinity schools, and for authors of books on Christian doctrine. In everyday talk, people often say he's a theologian to mean he thinks deeply about God, usually with a little admiration. The word is used across denominations, but Catholics and Orthodox often apply it more narrowly to people with formal training or authority.

distinctions.note: A pastor leads and cares for a congregation, while a theologian focuses on study and teaching of doctrine, though one person can be both.
A philosopher of religion analyzes religious concepts with general philosophical tools, while a theologian works within a particular faith tradition and its sources.

examples.everyday: My friend Mark is a theologian at the seminary, so I always ask him about faith questions over coffee.
examples.professional: We invited a theologian from the divinity school to speak to the church staff about the new study curriculum.
examples.analytical: The theologian argues that divine omniscience and human freedom must be understood together rather than as competing claims.

nuance.analogy: A theologian is like a structural engineer for belief: they examine how the parts of doctrine hold together and where the load-bearing beams are.
nuance.etymology: From Greek theologos, 'one who speaks of God,' from theos 'god' and logos 'word, discourse.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'theologist,' which is rare and sounds unnatural; use theologian.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'thee-uh-LOH-jee-un' instead of ending with a short 'jun' sound.

traditions.view: Orthodox tradition uses theologian in a deeper sense, for someone who knows God through prayer and purification, as in the title 'John the Theologian.' Formal academic study is valued but is not the main test.
A theologian is usually a trained scholar who works in service to the Church's teaching, and the magisterium holds final authority over official doctrine.

Protestants generally see a theologian as accountable to Scripture and the community of faith, with authority varying by denomination; Reformed, Lutheran, Baptist and Anglican scholars often differ on method and emphasis.

senses.definition: The study of God, a god, or gods; and of the truthfulness of religion in general.
senses.example: She studied theology at seminary before becoming a hospital chaplain.

senses.definition: Synonym of religious studies.
senses.example: Her university offers theology courses covering Buddhism, Islam, and Judaism.

senses.definition: An organized method of interpreting spiritual works and beliefs into practical form.
senses.example: The church's theology guides how members serve their neighbors each week.

senses.definition: A particular belief within a religion.
senses.example: Their theology holds that salvation comes through faith alone.

senses.definition: Subjective marginal details.
senses.example: Her notes were full of personal theology scribbled in the margins.

core.definition: The systematic study of God, religious faith and belief, and the nature of religious truth.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on AH, the second syllable. The middle syllable is reduced to a weak 'luh', and the final -gy is pronounced as 'jee', not as a hard 'g'. Begin with a voiceless th, as in 'thin', not 't'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In religious settings it is respectful, but in casual talk it can suggest abstract or dense thinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use theology in churches, seminaries, Bible colleges, and books about religion. In casual conversation, people also ask someone's theology, meaning what they believe about God. For a general interest in faith, people more often say religion or faith, and theology is used when the discussion is systematic or doctrinal.

distinctions.note: Religion refers to faith, practice and community in general, while theology is the systematic and reasoned study of God and religious truth.
Religious studies is a broad, often descriptive academic field that examines many religions, while theology is usually done from within a faith tradition and seeks to understand its truths.
Philosophy of religion asks general questions about God and religious claims using philosophical methods, while theology draws on scripture, tradition and doctrine.

examples.everyday: My sister is studying theology at seminary, so she always has big questions at dinner.
examples.professional: Our nonprofit's mission draws on Catholic social theology, so we check every new program against those principles.
examples.analytical: Systematic theology attempts to arrange the church's teachings about God, creation and salvation into a coherent whole.

nuance.analogy: Theology is like a map of the territory of faith, drawn carefully so that the roads connect and the distances make sense.
nuance.etymology: From Greek theologia, from theos 'god' and logia 'discourse, study', from logos 'word'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the initial th as a t sound (TAY-oh) or as the name Theo, instead of a voiceless th.
Confusing theology with theosophy, which is a different esoteric movement.

theology.etymology: From Middle English *theologie*, from Middle French *theologie*, from Old French *theologie*, from Latin *theologia*, from Koine Greek *θεολογία*, from *θεολόγος*, from *θεός* + *λόγος*.

senses.definition: Concerned with theories or hypotheses rather than with practical matters.
Existing only in theory, not proven in reality.

core.definition: Concerned with theories or hypotheses rather than with practical matters; or existing only in theory and not proven in reality.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RET, and the first syllable of the ending is a short ih sound. The vowel in the middle is weak, so do not say thee-oh-RET-ik.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy, where it contrasts with practical reason. It can sound dismissive when used to say an idea has no practical value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say theoretical rather than theoretic in everyday speech. Theoretic appears mainly in philosophy, especially in phrases such as theoretic reason and theoretic knowledge, following Kant's usage. Using it in casual conversation may sound stiff or like a mistake, so prefer theoretical there.

distinctions.note: Theoretical is the everyday American form and is used much more widely; theoretic is restricted mainly to philosophical phrases.
Practical is the direct contrast, meaning useful in action, while theoretic means concerned with theory rather than action.

examples.everyday: That plan sounds nice, but it's pretty theoretic, so let's try it on a small batch first.
examples.professional: The model is still theoretic at this point, so we need a pilot before we promise anything to the client.
examples.analytical: Kant distinguishes theoretic reason, which seeks to know what is, from practical reason, which determines what ought to be done.

nuance.analogy: A theoretic idea is like a blueprint: it shows how the house could stand, but it has not yet been built.
nuance.etymology: From Greek theoretikos, contemplative, from theorein, to look at or contemplate.
common_mistakes: Using theoretic in casual American speech, where theoretical is the normal form.
Putting the stress on the first syllable, as in THEE-uh-RET-ik; the main stress falls on RET.

theoretic.etymology: English *theory* + *etic*, from Latin *theōrēticus*, from Ancient Greek *θεωρητικός*.

senses.definition: A hymn to Mary, the Theotokos, read or chanted during the Divine Services of the Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches.

core.definition: A hymn honoring Mary as Theotokos, the God-bearer, sung in Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic services.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, 'TOH'. The final '-ion' is an unstressed 'uhn', not 'on', and the 'eo' is pronounced as 'ee-oh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive within Orthodox and Eastern Catholic communities. To outsiders, it is a specialized liturgical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear this word in Orthodox, Byzantine Catholic, or Eastern Catholic parishes and in liturgical music. In Western churches people usually say 'a hymn to Mary' or 'a Marian hymn,' so be ready to explain the term if you use it. In a parish bulletin or choir practice, 'the theotokion' is a normal and precise way to refer to it.

distinctions.note: A troparion is a short hymn for a feast or saint, while a theotokion specifically honors the Theotokos.
A Marian hymn is a general term for any hymn to Mary, while a theotokion is a specific liturgical form in the Eastern tradition.
An akathist is a longer hymn service in honor of Christ or Mary, while a theotokion is a shorter hymn.

collocations: the theotokion in the eighth tone

examples.everyday: After the service, my friend explained the theotokion we had just sung for Mary.
examples.professional: Our parish choir practices the Sunday theotokion before each Vespers service.
examples.analytical: The theotokion, as a liturgical genre, places Mary within the Christological confession of Ephesus by praising her as the one who bore God.

nuance.analogy: A theotokion is like a short refrain sung to Mary, repeated in worship the way a chorus returns in a familiar song.
nuance.etymology: From Greek theotokos meaning God-bearer, the title of Mary, with the Greek suffix -ion.
common_mistakes: Ending the word with 'on' (thee-oh-TOH-kee-on) instead of the unstressed 'uhn'.
Confusing theotokion, a hymn, with Theotokos, the title of Mary.
nuance.biblical_note: The title Theotokos rests on Luke 1:43, where Elizabeth greets Mary as the mother of her Lord, the Greek word being kyrios. Luke 1:35 adds that the child will be called holy and the Son of God, which the church later used to support the title. The word theotokion itself does not appear in Scripture.

traditions.view: Theotokia are central to Orthodox worship, sung at Vespers, Matins and the Divine Liturgy. They honor Mary as Theotokos, affirming the full union of God and man in Christ.

Catholics honor Mary as Mother of God, a title affirmed at the Council of Ephesus in 431, and sing Marian hymns. The Latin rite does not use the theotokion as a liturgical genre, though Eastern Catholic churches do.

Most Protestant churches accept Mary as the mother of Jesus and see the title Mother of God as a statement about Christ's divinity. They generally do not sing hymns to Mary or pray to her, though Lutheran and Anglican practice varies more than Reformed and Baptist practice.

senses.definition: A polite way to dismiss thanks as unnecessary.
senses.example: You drove me to the airport? Thank you so much! Oh, please, think nothing of it.

core.definition: A polite reply to thanks or an apology, meaning it was no trouble or no big deal.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on NUTH in nothing, and reduce of to uhv. The it is short and quick, so say 'uh-DIT' with a flapped t in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm. It shows modesty and makes the other person feel at ease.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Oh, think nothing of it' after someone thanks them for a small favor, such as holding a door or giving a ride. It can also answer an apology when the mistake was minor. For a larger favor, a more natural reply is 'Happy to help' or 'Anytime'.

distinctions.note: You're welcome is the standard reply, while think nothing of it is warmer and more modest, suggesting the favor was small.
Don't mention it is very similar and equally casual, so both are interchangeable in everyday speech.
No problem is more casual and can sound dismissive for a serious inconvenience, while think nothing of it is more gracious.

antonyms: make a big deal of it
collocations: think nothing of it, it was no trouble

examples.everyday: Thanks for grabbing my package for me. Oh, think nothing of it.
examples.professional: Thanks for covering my shift yesterday. Think nothing of it, I was happy to help.
examples.analytical: Her thanks was sincere, but she was quick to say she thought nothing of it, which showed her humility.

nuance.analogy: Like handing back a coin someone dropped and waving off their thanks with a smile.
nuance.etymology: Think from Old English thencan, and nothing from Old English nan thing, meaning not any thing.
common_mistakes: Saying 'think nothing about it' instead of 'think nothing of it'.
Using it as a reply to a serious apology, where a warmer or more direct response is better.

senses.definition: To hitchhike.

core.definition: To hitchhike: stand by a road with your thumb out and ask drivers to give you a free ride.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RIDE, and a reduces to uh. Keep the r retroflex and the b silent. Learners often stress thumb, but the main stress is on the last word of the phrase.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly risky; it can suggest adventure or carelessness, and many Americans see it as unsafe.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thumb a ride in casual talk about getting a lift from a stranger, usually in a past story. Hitchhiking is rare today, so saying you thumbed a ride may surprise people or prompt a safety comment. A natural reply is Wow, were you scared? or Did you get there okay?

distinctions.note: Hitchhike is the neutral verb for the whole activity, while thumb a ride focuses on the gesture of getting a ride.
Hitch a ride is a little more casual and can also mean catching a lift from a friend or acquaintance.

collocations: thumb a ride to the airport
thumb a ride on the interstate
thumb a ride with a trucker
thumb a ride out of town

examples.everyday: Our car died on the way to the lake, so we thumbed a ride into town with a farmer.
examples.professional: After her rental broke down, the sales rep had to thumb a ride to the client site.
examples.analytical: To thumb a ride is to trust strangers with your safety, an act that reveals as much about the driver's character as about the hitchhiker's need.

nuance.analogy: Like holding up a sign that says going my way? using only your thumb.
nuance.etymology: Thumb is from Old English thūma; ride is from Old English ridan, to ride.
common_mistakes: Saying hitchhike a ride, since hitchhike is intransitive and needs no object.
Using thumb as a noun for a ride instead of the verb thumb a ride.

senses.definition: Very loud; that sounds like thunder; thundersome. Also in metaphorical expressions, signifying fury.

core.definition: Very loud, like thunder; powerful and rumbling in sound.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is weak and the final -ous is pronounced us, not oos, so say THUN-der-us.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive for applause or music; negative when describing anger, noise or threat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use thunderous with applause, a roar or footsteps in everyday speech. It is more vivid than loud and often suggests a crowd or force. Thunderous applause is a natural phrase to describe a crowd reaction at a concert or speech.

distinctions.note: Deafening means loud enough to prevent hearing, while thunderous stresses a powerful, rumbling quality.
Booming describes a deep, resonant sound, while thunderous suggests something overwhelming and dramatic.

examples.everyday: The crowd gave the band a thunderous ovation after the encore.
examples.professional: The product demo got thunderous applause from the sales team.
examples.analytical: The thunderous certainty of the old sermon left little room for doubt or lament.

nuance.analogy: Like a freight train passing close enough to shake the ground.
nuance.etymology: From thunder plus the adjective suffix -ous, from Latin -osus.
common_mistakes: Using thunder as an adjective, such as thunder applause, instead of thunderous applause.
Saying the middle syllable clearly as THUN-der-ous with a full oo vowel at the end.

senses.definition: Trees in a forest regarded as a source of wood.
senses.example: collect timber

senses.definition: Wood that has been pre-cut and is ready for use in construction.
senses.example: The contractor ordered fresh timber for the new deck and porch railings.

senses.definition: A heavy wooden beam, generally a whole log that has been squared off and used to provide heavy support for something such as a roof.
senses.example: the timbers of a ship

senses.definition: Material for any structure.
senses.example: Trust is the timber on which every good friendship is built.

senses.definition: The wooden stock of a rifle or shotgun.
senses.example: The rifle's walnut timber was scratched from years of hunting trips.

senses.definition: The stumps.
senses.example: Only the old timber remained after the clearcut, a field of stumps.

senses.definition: Used by loggers to warn others that a tree being felled is falling.
senses.example: Timber! Everybody clear out, that big oak is coming down.

senses.definition: A cry used when anything is falling over.
senses.example: Timber! The ladder slipped and the bookshelf toppled over onto the floor.

senses.definition: To fit with timbers.
senses.example: timbering a roof

senses.definition: To light or land on a tree.
senses.example: The hawk timbered on the highest branch of the dead pine.

senses.definition: To surmount as a timber does.
senses.example: The horse timbered the fence cleanly and galloped on across the field.

core.definition: Trees grown in forests, or wood cut and prepared for building, such as lumber or heavy beams.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the 'b' clearly, as in 'limber'. Do not drop the 'b' and say 'timer'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word for wood and forests, with a rural or traditional feel in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'timber' for standing trees in a forest and for large cut pieces of wood, especially in logging and construction. For smaller sawn boards, they say 'lumber'. Loggers shout 'Timber!' to warn that a falling tree is coming down, and the word also serves as a verb meaning to fit with timbers.

distinctions.note: Lumber is cut and sawn wood ready for building; timber can mean standing trees or large beams, not just boards.
Wood is the general material and can mean firewood or a small forest; timber is more specific to trees and construction.

examples.everyday: The old barn is made of heavy timber, and it has stood for more than a century.
examples.professional: The timber harvest is scheduled for the spring, and prices may shift with the lumber market.
examples.analytical: Scripture describes cedar and cypress timber brought from Lebanon for the Temple, so the material carries both practical and symbolic weight.

nuance.analogy: Timber is like the skeleton of a building: standing in the forest it is a living structure, and once cut it holds up the house.
nuance.etymology: From Old English timber, meaning building or building material; from Proto-Germanic *timrą, building.
common_mistakes: Dropping the 'b' in the pronunciation, so the word sounds like 'timer'.
Using 'timber' for a single board; 'lumber' or 'board' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, timber is usually translated from 'ets, meaning tree or wood. First Kings 5 and 6 describe cedar and cypress timber from Lebanon used for Solomon's Temple. Habakkuk 2:11 uses the image of a beam from the woodwork answering the cry of a stone, showing wood as part of the building's life.

timber.etymology: From Middle English *tymber*, from Old English *timber*, from **timr*, from Proto-Germanic **timrą* (“building; timber”), from Proto-Indo-European **dem-* (“to build; to arrange”).

senses.definition: To make someone tired; to exhaust.

core.definition: To make someone very tired, or become exhausted, especially from physical activity or long effort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on out, and tire is weaker. In fast speech, the r in tire links to out, so it often sounds like 'tie-rowt.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, since being tired out suggests you have no energy left.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tire out for children, pets, athletes, or people after a long day, as in 'The hike tired me out.' With people, tire out is the transitive form and needs an object, while tired out is the adjective. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I'm totally wiped out.'

distinctions.note: Wear out is common for people and objects; tire out focuses on making a person tired.
Exhaust is more formal and stronger, suggesting complete depletion of energy.
Drain suggests gradual loss of energy, often emotionally, while tire out describes physical or mental tiredness from activity.

examples.everyday: Let's go to the park so the kids can tire themselves out before bedtime.
examples.professional: Back-to-back meetings tire people out, so let's shorten the review to thirty minutes.
examples.analytical: Long theological debates can tire out participants, leaving the question itself unresolved.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone battery draining after a long day of use: the energy is gone, and it needs a recharge.
nuance.etymology: Tire comes from Middle English tiren, to weary; out adds the sense of completely.
common_mistakes: Using tire out without an object, as in 'I tire out after lunch,' which should be 'I get tired out' or 'I'm tired.'
Saying 'The hike tired out me' instead of 'The hike tired me out.'

senses.definition: Equivalent retribution; an act of returning exactly what one gets; an eye for an eye.
senses.example: If you hit me, I’ll hit you back; tit for tat.

core.definition: An act of returning the same harm or insult that someone gave you, in kind.

pronunciation.tip: Both TIT and TAT are stressed, and 'for' reduces to a quick 'fer'. Link the words smoothly, so it sounds like 'TIT-fer-TAT'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes retaliation, and it often suggests a petty back-and-forth rather than a fair response.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tit for tat' in casual conversation and news reporting, often about political or personal conflicts, as in 'It's tit for tat between the two parties.' It is informal and can be used with the verb 'to be' or 'to play.' A natural reply is 'Well, they started it.'

distinctions.note: Revenge is a broader, often stronger desire to hurt someone back. Tit for tat specifically describes a matching exchange of actions.
An eye for an eye is a more formal, moral phrase often used in discussions of justice. Tit for tat is more casual and focuses on the back-and-forth.

examples.everyday: My neighbor blocked our driveway, so I parked in his spot, and now it's just tit for tat.
examples.professional: The two teams have been in a tit-for-tat argument over deployment access, and nobody is making progress.
examples.analytical: The author warns that a tit-for-tat logic can turn a local dispute into a cycle of escalating injury.

nuance.analogy: Tit for tat is like a ping-pong match where each side hits the ball back exactly as hard as it came.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'for' as a full word 'for' with a strong vowel; in speech it is a reduced 'fer'.
Writing 'tit-for-tat' without hyphens when it is used as an adjective; American style usually hyphenates the adjective form.

tit-for-tat.etymology: conjectured to be ultimately from Dutch *dit voor dat* (“this for that”) or French *tant pour tant* (“equal for equal”).

senses.definition: Serving as a token of support, compliance, etc. but lacking substance; exhibiting or relating to tokenism.
senses.example: The government has taken nothing more than tokenistic actions on behalf of people with disabilities.

core.definition: Done only as a token, showing support or compliance in form but lacking real substance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NIS, the third syllable, not on TOH. The ending -istic is pronounced 'ISS-tik', with a short i and a light final k.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that a gesture is empty or insincere.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tokenistic in journalism, academic writing, and debates about policy or workplace inclusion. It usually describes actions, policies or gestures rather than people. In casual speech people more often say it's just for show.

distinctions.note: Symbolic is neutral and can mean meaningful; tokenistic is negative and means shallow or insincere.
Token as an adjective can mean minimal or nominal, but tokenistic adds the sense of a deliberate show of inclusion.
Superficial is general and means shallow; tokenistic is specifically about symbolic gestures that replace real change.

examples.everyday: Putting one photo of a Latino family in the brochure felt tokenistic to me.
examples.professional: The vendor's diversity training was tokenistic, since nothing changed in how we recruit or promote.
examples.analytical: A tokenistic response to inequality can make an institution look reformed while leaving its structures intact.

nuance.analogy: Like a fake storefront in a movie set: it looks like a real shop from the front, but nothing is inside.
nuance.etymology: From token, from Old English tācen, sign, plus the suffixes -ist and -ic.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'TOH-kuh-nis-tik'.
Using tokenistic to describe people; it is usually applied to actions or policies.
Confusing it with token, which as an adjective means minimal but not necessarily insincere.

senses.definition: A barrier across a toll road or toll bridge that is lifted when the toll is paid.
To furnish (a road) with a tollgate.
senses.example: The county council voted to tollgate the new bridge to pay for its repairs.

senses.definition: To perpetrate a form of corruption in which the recipient of a government contract must donate part of its value to the government.
senses.example: The contractor admitted he had been asked to tollgate a share of every road project payment.

core.definition: A barrier across a toll road or toll bridge that lifts when the driver pays the toll.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TOLL, and gate is secondary. The final sound is a clear, long a, as in gate, with a hard g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a factual, everyday term, but the verb sense is rare and carries a negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tollgate as the everyday word for the arm that lifts at a toll road, and they also say toll gate as two words. The verb form, meaning to take a kickback from a government contract, is rare and mostly appears in policy writing or news about corruption. In conversation, people say 'the toll gate is stuck' or 'we're at the tollgate.'

distinctions.note: A tollgate is the barrier that opens, while a tollbooth is the booth where the driver pays.
Toll barrier is a more technical synonym for tollgate, which is the common American word.

examples.everyday: The tollgate arm stayed down for a minute, so the car behind us almost hit the back of ours.
examples.professional: We need to update the tollgate hardware on the north bridge before the new software goes live.
examples.analytical: Economists describe the tollgate as a point where a controlling party extracts payment for passage, which can become a source of rent-seeking.

nuance.analogy: Like a turnstile at a stadium that only turns after you show a valid ticket.
nuance.etymology: From toll, a tax, and gate, a movable barrier.
common_mistakes: Using tollgate for the building where you pay; that is a tollbooth.
Using the verb tollgate in everyday talk, where it sounds odd or accusatory.

senses.definition: Tending to totter.

core.definition: Tending to totter, or unsteady, weak and likely to fall, as in tottery legs or a tottery old chair.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TAH. The final -y is pronounced as a tense 'ee,' not a short 'ih,' in General American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative or descriptive. It suggests weakness and instability, often in a figurative or literary way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tottery' less often than 'tottering.' It appears mostly in descriptive or literary writing about old people, furniture or fragile structures. In everyday speech, 'shaky' or 'wobbly' is more natural, so use 'tottery' when you want a vivid, slightly literary tone.

distinctions.note: Tottering describes an ongoing wobble in progress, while tottery describes a general quality or tendency to be unsteady.
Shaky is more common and can refer to nerves or trembling, while tottery stresses the risk of falling over.

examples.everyday: Grandpa's legs felt a little tottery after the long hike, so he sat down.
examples.professional: Their tottery startup depended on a single client to cover payroll.
examples.analytical: The poem's tottery syntax mirrors the speaker's loss of composure.

nuance.analogy: Like a wooden stool with one leg slightly loose.
nuance.etymology: From 'totter' plus the suffix '-y,' meaning having the quality of.
common_mistakes: Using 'tottery' in casual talk where 'shaky' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the final -y as a short 'ih' sound.

senses.definition: A similar vehicle for carrying materials.
senses.example: The mine's ore tram rattled down the mountain carrying copper to the rail yard.

senses.definition: A people mover.
An aerial cable car.
A train with wheels that runs on a road; a trackless train.
senses.example: We rode the tram from downtown to the waterfront, past the old brick warehouses.

senses.definition: A silk thread formed of two or more threads twisted together, used especially for the weft, or cross threads, of the best quality of velvets and silk goods.
senses.example: The weaver bought fine tram silk for the weft of the velvet upholstery.

senses.definition: To operate, or conduct the business of, a tramway.
senses.example: The company decided to tram the coastal route, running electric cars every ten minutes.

senses.definition: To travel by tram.
senses.example: We decided to tram to the stadium instead of driving through the downtown traffic.

senses.definition: To transport (material) by tram.
senses.example: The quarry crew would tram the crushed gravel down to the loading dock each morning.

senses.definition: To align a component in mechanical engineering or metalworking, particularly the spindle of a mill or drill press, as historically accomplished using a trammel.
senses.example: The machinist had to tram the mill spindle carefully before cutting the steel block.

senses.definition: To weave in this manner.
senses.example: The old loom operator trammed the silk into a thick, lustrous velvet pattern.

core.definition: An enclosed cable car or electric people mover that carries passengers along a set route, such as at a ski resort or airport.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short a from 'cat' and end with a clear m. Do not add a vowel after the m, and keep the tr sound quick, without a separate 't' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it describes a vehicle or transit system with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'tram' usually means an aerial tramway or an airport or park people mover, such as the tram to a ski summit. City rail cars that run on street tracks are called 'streetcars' or 'trolleys'; in British English, 'tram' is the city rail car. The verb sense, to travel by tram, is rare in American speech; Americans say 'ride the tram'.

distinctions.note: A streetcar is the American city rail vehicle on street tracks, which is the British tram; a tram in American usage is usually an aerial or people-mover system.
A cable car is pulled by a moving cable, often on steep city hills; an American tram is usually a larger aerial system or an airport people mover.
A gondola is a small enclosed cabin on a cable, often on ski lifts; a tram usually carries more people in a bigger car.

examples.everyday: Let's take the tram up to the top and ski down from there.
examples.professional: Our campus shuttle and tram route will change during the renovation next month, so please check the new schedule.
examples.analytical: Urban planners often treat the tram as a test of whether public transit can shape how a city grows.

nuance.analogy: An aerial tram is like an elevator that runs sideways through the sky: a fixed route, a large cabin, and many people sharing the ride.
nuance.etymology: Originally a beam or shaft; likely from Middle Dutch traem, meaning beam, with the vehicle sense developing later.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tram' for a city street rail car in most American cities; say 'streetcar' or 'light rail'.
Pronouncing the vowel as a long 'a' as in 'name' instead of the short a in 'cat'.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to a transition.
senses.example: transitional justice

senses.definition: Temporary; pending the implementation of something new.
senses.example: XHTML 1.0 Transitional

core.definition: Relating to a change from one state or condition to another; temporary while something new is put in place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZISH, and the -shun- syllable is reduced to uh. The final -al is a light, quick -ul, with no separate vowel sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it suggests change in progress and can be positive when it means growth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transitional in speech about life phases, policies, housing, and jobs, as in transitional housing or a transitional period. It sounds more formal than in-between. It is a common term in education and social services.

distinctions.note: Transitory emphasizes brevity and passing away; transitional emphasizes being a bridge between two states.
Interim describes a temporary position or arrangement; transitional more often describes a process of change.

examples.everyday: We are in a transitional phase right now since I just moved to Denver and started a new job.
examples.professional: Our transitional plan keeps the old API running until every client migrates to version two.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the modern self as a transitional figure, caught between tradition and secular individualism.

nuance.analogy: A transitional phase is like a bridge: you are not on either bank yet, but you are clearly crossing.
nuance.etymology: From transition, from Latin transitio, a going across.
common_mistakes: Stressing the -shun- syllable instead of ZISH
Using transitional to mean only temporary, when it stresses change between states

senses.definition: One who, or that which, trembles.
Any of various New World passerine birds of the genus Cinclocerthia.
senses.example: We spotted a trembler hopping along the forest floor in Costa Rica.

senses.definition: The vibrating hammer, or spring contact piece of a hammer break, as of the electric ignition apparatus for an internal combustion engine.
senses.example: The mechanic replaced the worn trembler on the ignition coil to fix the rough idle.

senses.definition: A kind of security alarm triggered by vibrations or shock waves.
senses.example: The store installed a trembler on the display case that rang when someone touched the glass.

core.definition: A person or thing that trembles, shaking quickly and lightly, usually from fear, cold or a vibration.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the short E in 'bed'. The bl cluster is quick, and the final -ler is a syllabic L with a light schwa, not two separate vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, usually suggesting nervousness, fear or weakness. It can also be purely descriptive for a machine part.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use trembler in everyday speech; they would say someone who is shaking or trembling. You will see it mainly in literary writing, or in older technical writing about electrical parts in engines. Use the verb tremble or the word shaking in normal conversation.

distinctions.note: Shaker is the common American word for a person or device that shakes, while trembler is rarer and more literary.
A tremor is a slight, involuntary shaking, often medical or seismic, while a trembler is a person or thing that trembles.

examples.everyday: The old puppy was a little trembler during thunderstorms, so we sat with him on the couch.
examples.professional: The older ignition system used a trembler, a vibrating contact that kept producing sparks.
examples.analytical: In the poem, the speaker is less a sturdy witness than a trembler, whose voice reveals fear before any argument can form.

nuance.analogy: A trembler is like a leaf in a breeze, moving quickly and lightly under a force it cannot control.
nuance.etymology: From tremble plus the suffix -er, meaning one who or that which trembles.
common_mistakes: Using trembler in everyday conversation, where someone who is shaking is more natural.
Confusing trembler with tremor, which is the more common noun for a shaking motion.

senses.definition: (rare) Trembling with fear or emotion.
senses.example: The trepidant student stood at the podium, hands trembling before the first question.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Nervous or fearful, trembling with anxiety or apprehension about what may happen.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowels are reduced, so the word has three quick syllables, with the final 'ant' weakened to 'dunt'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes fear or anxiety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use trepidant in speech. It appears occasionally in literary writing or deliberately old-fashioned prose. In everyday American English, say 'nervous', 'anxious' or 'apprehensive'. The more common related word is trepidatious, which is informal and playful.

distinctions.note: Trepidant is an adjective describing a person in a fearful state, while trepidation is a noun for the feeling itself.
Apprehensive is common and neutral in tone; trepidant is rare, literary and more emotionally vivid.

examples.everyday: She sounded a little trepidant when she called to ask about the test results.
examples.professional: The trepidant team waited for the audit report, unsure what it would reveal.
examples.analytical: The trepidant narrator of the novel hesitates at every threshold, unable to trust his own perceptions.

nuance.analogy: A trepidant person is like a leaf shaking in the wind before a storm, moved by a fear that has not yet arrived.
nuance.etymology: From Latin trepidans, present participle of trepidare, to be alarmed.
common_mistakes: Using trepidant in casual conversation, where 'nervous' is far more natural.
Confusing trepidant (adjective) with trepidation (noun), as in 'She felt trepidant' instead of 'She felt trepidation'.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to troglodytes, or dwellers in caves.
senses.example: The troglodytic cave dwellers of the valley had carved homes into the soft sandstone.

senses.definition: Like or befitting a troglodyte; brutish, backwards, etc.
